AI.motivation: Enterprises are deploying autonomous AI agents faster than they can govern them, with current approaches stretching single-discipline methods across all scales of agency, leading to governance gaps and production failures.
AI.method: CASE framework assigns: Control theory to individual agents, complex Adaptive systems theory to agent collectives, Supervisory cybernetics to human-agent teams, and Engineering operations to fleets. The authors formalize each layer, derive cross-layer coupling conditions, and validate with three empirical studies on production failures, ecosystem tools, and public deployments.
AI.result: Findings show: 82% of production agent failures are multi-layer trajectories; none of 22 ecosystem tools offer full Layer 2 (emergence) coverage; all 35 scored public deployments fall in lowest maturity band, revealing an "Emergence Gap" between risks and capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents a five-level maturity model with bottleneck-weighted index to operationalize CASE as scientific maturity model, addressing the need for architectures that satisfy requisite variety for effective human oversight required by regulations like EU AI Act Article 14.

title: Detecting Soft Skills in ML Engineering Roles CVs
summary: Soft skills shape collaboration among ML engineers, data scientists, and software engineers building ML-enabled systems, yet what we know about them comes almost entirely from the demand side. Job advertisements, surveys, and hiring manager interviews capture what employers ask for. How candidates themselves articulate these competencies has not been studied, and existing CV-mining work is both keyword-based, so it cannot see skills conveyed through narrative, and descriptive, reporting frequency rankings without testing whether group differences exceed sampling variation. We close both gaps. Using a balanced corpus of 300 curated CVs spanning the three roles, we extract explicitly listed and implicitly narrated soft skills with an LLM-based pipeline validated against a human-annotated ground truth, a distinction that existing extractors were not designed to make. We then convert the demand-side literature's claims into 13 falsifiable hypotheses about role signatures, seniority progression, and disclosure style, and test them with effect sizes under family-wise error control, so that candidate-side data can corroborate or contradict the demand-side account rather than merely illustrate it. Eleven hypotheses are supported, one partially, and one refuted. Candidates disclose soft skills through narrative rather than keyword lists by roughly three to one, and most so for the competencies employers value most: leadership, coordination, and mentoring (88-96% narrative). Seniority nearly triples the odds of articulating leadership. That competency, assumed universal in prior work, is articulated by software engineers at half the rate of their peers. Technical candidates do articulate soft skills, but a keyword-based screening systematically misses them.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how ML engineers, data scientists, and software engineers articulate soft skills in their CVs using LLM-based extraction, finding that candidates primarily use narrative rather than keyword lists, with significant role differences that contradict demand-side assumptions.
AI.motivation: Current understanding of soft skills in ML/tech roles comes almost entirely from employer perspectives (demand side), with little research on how candidates themselves articulate these competencies. Existing CV-mining approaches are keyword-based and descriptive, missing narrative expressions of skills and failing to test hypotheses about group differences.
AI.method: Used a balanced corpus of 300 curated CVs across ML engineers, data scientists, and software engineers. Developed an LLM-based pipeline to extract both explicitly listed and implicitly narrated soft skills, validated against human-annotated ground truth. Converted demand-side literature claims into 13 falsifiable hypotheses and tested them with effect sizes under family-wise error control.
AI.result: 11 hypotheses supported, 1 partially supported, 1 refuted. Candidates disclose soft skills through narrative rather than keyword lists by roughly 3:1 ratio. Narrative disclosure highest for leadership, coordination, and mentoring (88-96%). Seniority nearly triples odds of articulating leadership. Software engineers articulate leadership at half the rate of their ML/data science peers. Keyword-based screening systematically misses soft skill expressions.
AI.conclusion: Technical candidates do articulate soft skills, but current keyword-based screening methods systematically miss these competencies when expressed narratively. The study reveals important role-specific differences (software engineers articulate leadership less frequently) and highlights the need for better skill extraction methods that capture narrative expressions to align hiring practices with candidate self-representation.

title: SBCO: Self-Supervised, Verifier-Grounded Harness Optimization For Planning Agents
summary: Self-improving agents seek to reduce the human engineering effort behind AI systems by enabling them to evolve and self-improve their performance over time. Recently, methods like the Darwin Gödel Machine and the Huxley Gödel Machine have been proposed which enable open-ended, recursive self-improvement through self-reference where a coding agent edits its own code. Such self-referential self-improvement methods require that the competence required to perform the task coincides or aligns well with the competence required for self-modification which is the case for coding tasks. For domains or tasks, which do not satisfy the alignment needed, self-referential self-improvement is not available. In such cases, it is possible to adapt the above algorithms to other tasks by removing the self-referential aspect or introducing explicit self-modification of a meta-agent -- both computationally expensive, relying on population or self-modification search over many candidate agents. For planning tasks with explicit constraints, we propose a far cheaper alternative. We introduce SBCO (Self-supervised Block Coordinate Optimizer), a verifier-grounded harness optimizer in the same closed-loop, improve-from-experience family as the Gödel-machine methods, but self-supervised rather than self-referential. Given an agentic harness, SBCO learns a decomposed bank of verifiers and a harness policy via approximate block coordinate ascent, improving the agent's outputs from its own graded feedback---with a fixed meta-agent and no human labels. Across two domains SBCO matches or exceeds a customized self-modifying baseline while using 4-5.5 times less compute budget.

AI.tldr: SBCO is a self-supervised optimizer that improves agent performance through verifier-grounded learning without self-modification, using less compute than self-referential methods.
AI.motivation: Existing self-improving methods like Darwin/Huxley Gödel Machines require alignment between task competence and self-modification competence, limiting applicability. For tasks without this alignment, current alternatives are computationally expensive, relying on population search or meta-agent self-modification.
AI.method: SBCO (Self-supervised Block Coordinate Optimizer) uses a verifier-grounded approach with approximate block coordinate ascent to learn a decomposed bank of verifiers and harness policy. It operates in a closed-loop, improve-from-experience framework but is self-supervised rather than self-referential, requiring no human labels or self-modifying meta-agent.
AI.result: Across two domains, SBCO matches or exceeds the performance of a customized self-modifying baseline while using 4-5.5 times less compute budget.
AI.conclusion: SBCO provides an efficient alternative to self-referential self-improvement methods for planning tasks with constraints, offering comparable performance with significantly lower computational cost, making self-improvement more accessible for domains where task and self-modification competences don't align.

title: Physics-Informed Machine Learning in Prognostics and Health Management: A Systematic Literature Review
comment: The version of record of this article, first published in Journal of Intelligent Manufacturing, is available online at: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10845-026-02930-3 . This arXiv version is content-equivalent but differs in four respects: (i) additional appendix; (ii) disambiguated citations; (iii) numbered section headings; and (iv) figures with selectable and searchable text
summary: In modern industry, keeping complex systems reliable, safe, and efficient hinges on Prognostics and Health Management (PHM). Machine Learning (ML) has largely driven advancements in diagnostics and prognostics, yet purely data-driven models face inherent limitations, such as poor generalization, an inability to infer causal relationships, and a lack of interpretability. Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) helps mitigate these limitations by incorporating prior physical knowledge directly into the ML pipeline, thereby fostering growing interest in its application to PHM. This work investigates how PIML is being leveraged in the context of PHM through a systematic literature review of 212 studies. The review introduces a four-class classification scheme, consisting of observational bias, inductive bias, learning bias, and hybrid approaches, and further categorizes studies by PHM task. Across all four classes, the reviewed studies consistently demonstrate improved predictive performance over conventional baselines across a broad range of assets, although the literature is heavily skewed toward lithium-ion batteries and bearings, and dominated by problem-specific solutions. Overall, the review indicates that physics-informed approaches already provide tangible benefits, whereas claims of improvements concerning some of the aforementioned limitations lack sufficient supporting evidence. Future research should prioritize transferable design patterns, benchmarks comparing integration strategies, and uncertainty-aware models that are lightweight and robust enough for online deployment in real-world settings.

AI.tldr: A systematic literature review of 212 studies on Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) for Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) showing consistent performance improvements over conventional methods, with classification into four approaches and identification of research gaps.
AI.motivation: Machine Learning has advanced PHM but pure data-driven models have limitations like poor generalization, inability to infer causality, and lack of interpretability. PIML helps mitigate these by incorporating physical knowledge into ML pipelines, prompting investigation of its applications in PHM.
AI.method: Conducted a systematic literature review of 212 studies, introduced a four-class classification scheme (observational bias, inductive bias, learning bias, and hybrid approaches), and categorized studies by PHM task type.
AI.result: Across all four PIML classes, reviewed studies consistently show improved predictive performance over conventional baselines across various assets. However, literature is heavily skewed toward lithium-ion batteries and bearings, dominated by problem-specific solutions with insufficient evidence supporting claims about causality and interpretability improvements.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed approaches provide tangible benefits in PHM, but future research should prioritize transferable design patterns, benchmarks comparing integration strategies, and uncertainty-aware models that are lightweight and robust for real-world online deployment.

title: Generating Attacks for LLMs with GFlowNets
summary: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has facilitated their ubiquitous integration into various domains, leading to widespread adoption. However, this escalating trend has introduced significant security vulnerabilities, necessitating the identification and mitigation of flaws arising from malicious exploitation. Red teaming assessments, conducted to evaluate model robustness through diverse adversarial inputs, are essential for exposing security risks and implementing countermeasures. Currently, red teaming is performed either manually by experts or automatically using predefined attack datasets. Nevertheless, manual testing remains time-consuming, while existing automated methods suffer from limited creativity due to their inherent dependency on fixed datasets. In this study, we propose an automated, human-independent, and adaptive approach leveraging GFlowNets to identify LLM vulnerabilities by utilizing one large language model to test another. Within this framework, an attacker model is trained against a specified victim model to perform automated red teaming and provide a quantitative robustness score. This research aims to generate more effective adversarial attacks in English compared to existing benchmarks and, as a novel contribution to the literature, introduces a model capable of generating attack inputs in the Turkish language.

AI.tldr: Automated LLM vulnerability testing using GFlowNets with attacker-victim model framework for adaptive, creative attacks in English and Turkish.
AI.motivation: Current LLM red teaming methods are either manual (time-consuming) or automated with fixed datasets (lacking creativity), creating security vulnerabilities that need more adaptive testing approaches.
AI.method: Proposes GFlowNets-based framework using one LLM to test another, where an attacker model is trained against a victim model to perform automated red teaming and compute quantitative robustness scores.
AI.result: Generates more effective adversarial attacks in English compared to existing benchmarks and introduces novel capability to generate attack inputs in Turkish language.
AI.conclusion: The proposed automated, human-independent, adaptive approach addresses limitations of current red teaming methods by enabling more creative and effective vulnerability discovery across multiple languages.

title: Observational Policy Ranking for SMB Financial Guidance from Multi-Action Accounting Logs
summary: Small and medium-sized businesses need timely financial guidance, yet historical accounting logs record self-selected and often co-occurring business changes rather than randomized recommendations. We formulate this setting as observational policy ranking: from pre-decision financial information, a policy selects one of 34 ledger-derived business-change categories for a target financial KPI. Using 85,078 company-month observations from 7,505 firms, we introduce Covariate-Adjusted Residual Policy Learning (CAR-PL), an action-wise R-learner that operates directly on multi-hot logs and regularizes selection by observational support. We compare CAR-PL with an uplift T-Learner, a conservative contextual value model, a zero-shot LLM, and non-personalized references on company-disjoint held-out firms under a shared model-assisted scoring rule. CAR-PL has the highest Gross Profit point estimate (0.084), the T-Learner has the highest Revenue point estimate (0.085), and the contextual value model has the highest Quick Ratio point estimate (0.062). CAR-PL and the T-Learner are not statistically separated on either growth KPI in matched company-clustered comparisons, while CAR-PL selects 33-34 categories and produces less concentrated selections across the catalog. Outcome-model-only scoring retains the same KPI-level point-estimate leader or top pair, and category rankings remain similar when the all-zero treatment reference is replaced by the most common training co-action pattern. These findings support objective-specific ranking of SMB financial guidance from multi-action accounting logs.

AI.tldr: CAR-PL (Covariate-Adjusted Residual Policy Learning) outperforms alternative methods for ranking business-change recommendations from accounting logs to improve SMB financial KPIs.
AI.motivation: Small and medium-sized businesses need timely financial guidance, but historical accounting logs record self-selected, co-occurring business changes rather than randomized recommendations, creating an observational policy ranking problem.
AI.method: The authors introduce CAR-PL, an action-wise R-learner that operates directly on multi-hot logs and regularizes selection by observational support. They compare it with an uplift T-Learner, a conservative contextual value model, a zero-shot LLM, and non-personalized references using 85,078 company-month observations from 7,505 firms.
AI.result: CAR-PL has the highest Gross Profit point estimate (0.084), the T-Learner has the highest Revenue point estimate (0.085), and the contextual value model has the highest Quick Ratio point estimate (0.062). CAR-PL selects 33-34 categories and produces less concentrated selections than alternatives.
AI.conclusion: The findings support objective-specific ranking of SMB financial guidance from multi-action accounting logs, with CAR-PL and T-Learner showing competitive performance on growth KPIs while maintaining broad recommendation coverage.

title: TRACE: Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Conversational Engine
summary: Public service chatbots are expected to deliver recommendations from an underlying public service directory, while also making sure that the recommendations respect explicit user constraints. In practice, public service directories are noisy and inconsistent, and general-purpose large language model (LLM) or AI-based chatbots frequently generate unreliable recommendations, citing unverified sources from the web. We investigate the impact of retrieval quality on constraint-aware recommendation in public service conversational systems built over noisy and heterogeneous service directories. We propose TRACE (Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Conversational Engine), a retrieval-based, constraint-aware framework that parses input user queries into structural and semantic constraints for downstream retrieval, with the help of a dual data representation schema. Using a curated statewide pantry directory and a synthetic query benchmark, we evaluate multiple knowledge-representation variants with and without knowledge graphs (KGs). We experiment with several open-source LLMs and a proprietary model, showing that strengthening retrieval substantially improves user constraint satisfaction while reducing hallucinated recommendations. Performance differences across LLMs narrowed in our experiments as retrieval quality improved, making results less sensitive to model size. These findings suggest that the quality of retrieval is key for robust public service conversational systems.

AI.tldr: TRACE framework improves public service chatbot recommendations by enhancing retrieval quality with dual data representation, reducing hallucinations and improving constraint satisfaction regardless of LLM size.
AI.motivation: Public service chatbots often generate unreliable recommendations due to noisy service directories and general-purpose LLMs hallucinating from unverified web sources. There's a need for constraint-aware recommendation systems that can handle heterogeneous, inconsistent data while respecting user constraints.
AI.method: Proposed TRACE (Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Conversational Engine), a retrieval-based framework that parses user queries into structural and semantic constraints using a dual data representation schema. Evaluated multiple knowledge-representation variants with/without knowledge graphs (KGs) using open-source and proprietary LLMs on a curated pantry directory and synthetic query benchmark.
AI.result: Strengthening retrieval substantially improves user constraint satisfaction while reducing hallucinated recommendations. Performance differences across LLMs narrowed as retrieval quality improved, making results less sensitive to model size.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval quality is key for robust public service conversational systems, with improved retrieval enabling better constraint satisfaction and reduced hallucinations regardless of the underlying LLM's size.

title: ChronoSSM: Training for Temporally Aware Representations in Autoregressive State Space Models
summary:
Modern sequence models, from Transformers to State Space Models, have enabled powerful generative modeling across diverse domains, yet they are typically trained to predict what happens while treating when it happens as a secondary concern. In data-mining settings where events are associated with explicit timing information, this separation can limit temporal reasoning, anomaly detection, and faithful reconstruction of event chronology. A common strategy is to treat timing as an auxiliary signal, training a separate timing model using representations learned solely for event prediction. However, this two-stage approach implicitly assumes that representations optimized for event prediction already contain sufficient temporal structure.
  We introduce ChronoSSM, an autoregressive State Space Model (SSM) that jointly models events and timestamps with a shared backbone trained using combined token and temporal generation objectives. We compare the joint regime, where temporal supervision updates the backbone, with the two-stage regime, where timing is learned only using the frozen event representations. Across four domains spanning dense and partial timestamp supervision, joint training consistently makes inter-arrival information more recoverable from frozen representations without any systematic degradation in content-generation quality overall. Our results show that temporal supervision can produce more temporally informative representations without materially degrading autoregressive event modeling.

AI.tldr: ChronoSSM is a State Space Model that jointly models events and timestamps with shared backbone training, showing that joint temporal supervision produces more temporally informative representations without harming event modeling quality.
AI.motivation: Current sequence models treat event prediction as primary and timing as secondary, limiting temporal reasoning, anomaly detection, and faithful event chronology reconstruction. Two-stage approaches assume event representations already contain sufficient temporal structure, which may not be true.
AI.method: ChronoSSM is an autoregressive State Space Model that jointly models events and timestamps with a shared backbone trained using combined token and temporal generation objectives. It compares joint training (where temporal supervision updates the backbone) with two-stage regimes (where timing is learned only using frozen event representations).
AI.result: Across four domains spanning dense and partial timestamp supervision, joint training consistently makes inter-arrival information more recoverable from frozen representations without systematic degradation in content-generation quality overall.
AI.conclusion: Temporal supervision can produce more temporally informative representations without materially degrading autoregressive event modeling, challenging the assumption that event-optimized representations already contain sufficient temporal structure.

title: Post-Hoc Sparse Coding of Latent Communication Between Vision-Language Model Agents
summary: Latent-space communication allows heterogeneous vision-language model agents to exchange continuous representations without serializing visual and reasoning states into text. Vision Wormhole realizes this approach by translating visual features into a universal latent representation that can be consumed by another model, but every message is transported as a dense tensor of the same size regardless of its content. A fixed-capacity dense tensor therefore need not have a fixed effective information density: some messages may use only a small fraction of the available representational degrees of freedom. This observation suggests that the communication channel may be substantially compressible. We study its redundancy by fitting a post-hoc sparse autoencoder to frozen Vision Wormhole activations and measuring reconstruction, downstream utility, feature reuse, and token-level interventions across nine reasoning benchmarks. Relative to the original float32 transport, a uint16-index/float16-value sparse payload with k=4 active coefficients per token reduces the transmitted bytes by 128x. In a single-run evaluation, the seven-task non-AIME mean accuracy changes from 49.85% to 49.77%. The fitted 4096-element dictionary uses only 50 features, and task-level active sets have a mean pairwise Jaccard similarity of 0.906. These measurements establish strong post-hoc compressibility relative to the original transport, but do not yet isolate the incremental contribution of sparse coding from position selection, reduced precision, low-rank structure, or SAE optimization effects. The results motivate matched-payload comparisons and communication mechanisms whose payload adapts to the information used by each message.

AI.tldr: Vision Wormhole's latent-space communication can be compressed 128x using sparse coding (k=4 active coefficients per token) with minimal accuracy loss, showing high redundancy in vision-language model agent communication.
AI.motivation: Vision Wormhole uses fixed-size dense tensors for latent-space communication between vision-language models, but these tensors likely have low effective information density for many messages, suggesting the communication channel may be highly compressible.
AI.method: Researchers fitted a post-hoc sparse autoencoder (SAE) to frozen Vision Wormhole activations, creating a 4096-element dictionary with sparse coding (k=4 active coefficients per token), using uint16 indices and float16 values to reduce payload size.
AI.result: Compression achieved 128x reduction in transmitted bytes (from float32 to sparse uint16/float16), with minimal accuracy change (49.85% to 49.77% on seven non-AIME tasks). The dictionary uses only 50 features, and task-level active sets show high similarity (mean Jaccard similarity 0.906).
AI.conclusion: Vision Wormhole's communication channel exhibits strong post-hoc compressibility, but more controlled experiments are needed to isolate sparse coding's specific contribution from other factors. Results suggest adaptive communication mechanisms where payload size matches message information content.

title: Procedural Fairness Failures in RLHF from Preference Averaging
comment: 4 pages, Accepted at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on Algorithmic Fairness Across Alignment Procedures and Agentic Systems (AFAA)
summary: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) aggregates heterogeneous preferences into a single reward model, assuming preference homogeneity. When preferences are heterogeneous, this aggregation induces a procedural fairness failure where majority preference groups dominate reward learning while minority preferences are systematically under-represented. This work defines procedural fairness in alignment as preserving distinct preference signals during reward modeling and shows that standard RLHF violates this via preference averaging. Preference-Aware RLHF (PA-RLHF) is introduced, separating optimization across preference modes at the reward learning stage. In a controlled setting, PA-RLHF improves overall alignment accuracy from 46.9% to 67.9% and reduces the fairness gap between best and worst aligned groups from 15.9 to 9.6 percentage points. These results show that procedural fairness failures in alignment can arise from structural design choices in reward learning, even in controlled, noise-free settings, with direct implications for large language models and agentic systems, where biased reward models can compound inequities across sequential decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Preference-Aware RLHF (PA-RLHF) to address fairness issues in standard RLHF when preferences are heterogeneous, showing improved alignment accuracy and reduced fairness gaps.
AI.motivation: Standard RLHF aggregates heterogeneous preferences into a single reward model, assuming preference homogeneity, which leads to procedural fairness failures where majority preference groups dominate while minority preferences are systematically under-represented.
AI.method: The paper introduces Preference-Aware RLHF (PA-RLHF) that separates optimization across preference modes at the reward learning stage, preserving distinct preference signals instead of averaging them.
AI.result: In a controlled setting, PA-RLHF improves overall alignment accuracy from 46.9% to 67.9% and reduces the fairness gap between best and worst aligned groups from 15.9 to 9.6 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Procedural fairness failures in alignment can arise from structural design choices in reward learning, even in controlled, noise-free settings, with direct implications for large language models and agentic systems where biased reward models can compound inequities across sequential decisions.

title: Edge Phoneme Recognition for Children's Speech through Age-Aware Training
comment: 3 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Demonstration paper presented at the non-archival demonstrations track of the 13th ACM Conference on Learning @ Scale (L@S '26), Seoul, South Korea, June 29-July 3, 2026. Not published in the ACM Digital Library
summary: Detecting phonemes from children's speech has historically been difficult due to the scarcity of training data, and unique characteristics of children's speech. During a phoneme detection competition, we found that training a lightweight model to predict the age of the learner, as well as the phoneme sequence, enabled a 94M-parameter model to outperform WavLM Large models (317M) on the target DrivenData distribution, and fall within approximately 0.04 CER of competition ensembles with 90 times the parameters. This has enabled the creation of PhonemeTrainer, an application that can run on most modern cellular phones. This will ultimately enable better Automated Speech Recognition (ASR) and pronunciation helper apps for children's speech, with the privacy and compliance benefits that come with edge processing.

AI.tldr: A lightweight 94M-parameter model using age prediction as an auxiliary task outperforms larger 317M models on children's phoneme detection, enabling mobile deployment for privacy-preserving speech recognition.
AI.motivation: There's a significant challenge in detecting phonemes from children's speech due to scarce training data and unique characteristics of children's speech, combined with the need for privacy-preserving solutions that can run on mobile devices.
AI.method: The authors trained a lightweight model (94M parameters) with dual objectives: predicting the age of the learner AND predicting phoneme sequences, using this multi-task learning approach to better handle children's speech characteristics.
AI.result: The lightweight model outperformed much larger WavLM Large models (317M parameters) on the target DrivenData distribution, and came within approximately 0.04 Character Error Rate (CER) of competition ensembles with 90 times more parameters. This enabled the creation of PhonemeTrainer, a mobile application.
AI.conclusion: The multi-task learning approach with age prediction as an auxiliary task enables effective phoneme detection for children's speech with lightweight models suitable for mobile deployment, providing privacy benefits through edge processing while maintaining competitive performance.

title: SeFoRA: Sketch-Aggregated Federated Low-Rank Adaptation with Heterogeneous Client Ranks
summary: We consider federated parameter efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks with low-rank adaptation (LoRA,~Hu et al.\ 2022). Combining LoRA with federated PEFT introduces challenges absent from either setting alone: clients may use different LoRA ranks, making their factor matrices dimension-incompatible, and factor-wise averaging suffers from a bilinear mismatch. We propose SeFoRA, a sketch-aggregated federated LoRA algorithm in which each client transmits a linear sketch of its local updates, enabling direct aggregation at the federator. As a result, SeFoRA alleviates the bilinear mismatch, and allows for aggregation in a small subspace of the full model. We introduce a rank-homogeneous version called SeFoRA-Ho which allows for direct adapter aggregation in this setting. We prove convergence to a neighborhood of the first-order stationary point at rate $\cO(1/T)$ for the rank-homogeneous setting. Numerical experiments on fine-tuning RoBERTa-Large on GLUE datasets show how our algorithms outperform the state-of-the-art.

AI.tldr: SeFoRA is a federated learning method that uses sketching to aggregate low-rank adaptation (LoRA) updates from clients, solving dimension incompatibility and bilinear mismatch problems in federated parameter efficient fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses challenges in federated parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) using LoRA, where two main problems arise: 1) clients may use different LoRA ranks making their factor matrices dimension-incompatible, and 2) factor-wise averaging suffers from a bilinear mismatch when combining updates from different clients.
AI.method: The authors propose SeFoRA (sketch-aggregated federated LoRA algorithm) where each client transmits a linear sketch of their local updates, enabling direct aggregation at the federator. They also introduce a rank-homogeneous version called SeFoRA-Ho for direct adapter aggregation in consistent rank settings.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis proves convergence to a neighborhood of the first-order stationary point at rate O(1/T) for the rank-homogeneous setting. Numerical experiments on fine-tuning RoBERTa-Large on GLUE datasets show that SeFoRA outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: SeFoRA effectively solves the fundamental challenges in federated LoRA by using sketching techniques, enabling practical federated parameter efficient fine-tuning while maintaining theoretical guarantees and empirical performance improvements.

title: Mitigating Bus Bunching with Reinforcement Learning Enhanced by Semantic Stop Embedding
summary: Bus bunching degrades service regularity and increases passenger waiting in high-frequency transit. Existing reinforcement-learning-based holding controllers primarily rely on instantaneous operational variables or route-specific stop identifiers, which provide limited information about the functional and operational context of individual stops and constrain policy reuse across routes. This study introduces an LLM-assisted semantic stop representation for event-driven bus holding control. An LLM is used offline to transform heterogeneous stop information, including physical attributes, surrounding activity context, and historical operational characteristics, into fixed semantic embeddings that are incorporated into a deep Q-learning controller without requiring real-time LLM inference. Experiments are conducted in stochastic simulations calibrated with observed data from two bus routes. Compared with the best calibrated Daganzo baseline, the semantic controller reduces headway variability, bunching events, and passenger waiting time by 32.0%, 69.2%, and 24.0%, respectively. A route-specific stop identifier does not improve the spacing-only controller, whereas semantic stop information improves headway regularity, waiting time, and holding effort, providing a more favorable overall trade-off across control objectives. Cross-route experiments further show that zero-shot transfer provides limited immediate generalization, while warm-start fine-tuning accelerates early-stage learning and improves transferred policies; cold-start training nevertheless achieves the best final performance. These findings suggest that semantic state representations can complement conventional operational states and support adaptation-based policy reuse across related transit routes.

AI.tldr: LLM-assisted semantic stop representation improves bus holding control by reducing headway variability (32%), bunching events (69%), and passenger waiting time (24%) compared to best baseline.
AI.motivation: Bus bunching degrades transit service regularity and increases passenger waiting. Existing reinforcement learning controllers rely on limited information (instantaneous variables or route-specific stop IDs), which constrains policy reuse across routes and provides insufficient functional/operational context.
AI.method: Uses LLM offline to transform heterogeneous stop information (physical attributes, surrounding activity context, historical operational characteristics) into fixed semantic embeddings. These are incorporated into a deep Q-learning controller for event-driven bus holding control without requiring real-time LLM inference. Experiments conducted in stochastic simulations calibrated with observed data from two bus routes.
AI.result: Semantic controller reduces headway variability by 32.0%, bunching events by 69.2%, and passenger waiting time by 24.0% compared to best calibrated Daganzo baseline. Route-specific stop identifiers don't improve spacing-only controller, while semantic stop information improves headway regularity, waiting time, and holding effort with better trade-off across objectives. Cross-route experiments show zero-shot transfer has limited generalization, warm-start fine-tuning accelerates early learning, but cold-start training achieves best final performance.
AI.conclusion: Semantic state representations can complement conventional operational states and support adaptation-based policy reuse across related transit routes, offering significant improvements in bus holding control performance.

title: The Evaluation Protocol Determines the Result: An Independent Reproduction of LeWorldModel on TwoRoom
summary:
LeWorldModel trains a latent world model with a prediction loss and a single anti-collapse regulariser, and reports approximately 87% of goals reached on TwoRoom, its simplest diagnostic environment. We reproduce that result by independent reimplementation on roughly $25 of rented compute, with all evaluation on one laptop CPU.
  We reach 94.0% at the repository's evaluation goal offset, against 84.0% for the authors' own released checkpoint measured under our protocol on identical episodes, and we reproduce the reported representation result directly (position probe Pearson r = 0.9988 against a reported 0.996). Reaching that point required four conventions that determine the outcome and appear in no released configuration file: dense action gathering across a frameskip block, a programmatically-set action-encoder width, ImageNet pixel normalisation, and action z-scoring. A reproducer following the released configurations alone obtains a model whose predictor cannot converge.
  The evaluation protocol is itself contested by the released material. The paper's appendix and the repository's configuration specify different goal offsets and step budgets; on the authors' own weights these yield 14.0% and 84.0%, and only the configuration's values reproduce the reported figure. On fifty identical episodes, changing nothing but how the goal is constructed moves that checkpoint from 84.0% to 8.0%.
  Two findings generalise. One-step prediction accuracy does not predict long-horizon planning success: across three checkpoints spanning a sevenfold range in prediction error, including the authors' own, it orders short-horizon success monotonically and fails to order long-horizon success at all. And a batch normalisation layer inflated our reported validation loss by up to a factor of 300, concealing a training loss that was flat throughout.

AI.tldr: LeWorldModel reproduction reveals critical undocumented implementation details affecting results, contests evaluation protocols, and highlights that one-step prediction accuracy doesn't predict long-horizon planning success.
AI.motivation: To independently verify and reproduce LeWorldModel's reported results, which claimed approximately 87% goal achievement on the TwoRoom environment, and to examine the robustness and reproducibility of the approach.
AI.method: Independent reimplementation with rented compute (~$25), reproduction attempts using released configurations, systematic testing of undocumented implementation conventions, comparison of evaluation protocols between paper and repository, and analysis across different checkpoints with varying prediction errors.
AI.result: Achieved 94.0% success rate (vs 84.0% for authors' checkpoint) by identifying four undocumented conventions; revealed inconsistencies in evaluation protocols yielding success rates from 8.0% to 84.0%; showed one-step prediction accuracy correlates with short-horizon but not long-horizon planning success; discovered batch normalization inflated validation loss by up to 300x.
AI.conclusion: LeWorldModel's reproducibility depends on undocumented implementation details, evaluation protocols are contested and inconsistent, and the fundamental assumption that one-step prediction accuracy predicts long-horizon planning success is questionable. The findings highlight reproducibility challenges in machine learning research.

title: Evaluation-Conditioned Training: Teaching Models to Generalize to Stronger Oversight Regimes
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures. Accepted at the Agent Behavior Workshop at COLM 2026. Code: https://github.com/evaluationconditionedtraining/Evaluation-Conditioned-Training
summary: Feedback signals used to train Large Language Models (LLMs) are the primary driver of their behavior and our main lever for instilling alignment with human values and objectives. However, a key limitation of current post-training methods is the inability of human annotators and automated reward functions to faithfully capture the feedback we would like to give. We introduce Evaluation-Conditioned Training (ECT), a post-training framework that uses natural language to condition each training sample on the fidelity of the feedback we provide and then elicits the desired behavior by conditioning the LLM on a high-fidelity monitor in deployment. ECT is aimed at improving performance under imperfect feedback and works as an add-on to existing algorithms such as SFT and PPO. We first provide a conceptual framework for ECT and discuss its potential to address persistent sources of reward mis-specification. Then we motivate ECT in the context of the eliciting latent knowledge (ELK) problem. Finally, we evaluate ECT on two proof-of-concept experiments: increasing even-handedness in news article generation and reducing sycophancy on an arithmetic task. In each setting, we utilize imperfect feedback, rewarding bias and agreement with the user, respectively. In both settings, ECT improves the targeted behavior relative to direct training.

AI.tldr: Evaluation-Conditioned Training (ECT) is a post-training framework that conditions LLMs on feedback fidelity using natural language, improving performance under imperfect feedback.
AI.motivation: Current post-training methods for LLMs suffer from limitations where human annotators and automated reward functions cannot faithfully capture desired feedback, creating issues with reward mis-specification and inability to elicit latent knowledge.
AI.method: ECT uses natural language to condition training samples on feedback fidelity, then elicits desired behavior by conditioning the LLM on high-fidelity monitors during deployment. It works as an add-on to existing algorithms like SFT and PPO.
AI.result: In proof-of-concept experiments: 1) Increased even-handedness in news article generation despite rewarding bias, and 2) Reduced sycophancy on arithmetic tasks despite rewarding agreement with users. ECT improved targeted behavior relative to direct training in both settings.
AI.conclusion: ECT addresses limitations of imperfect feedback in LLM alignment by conditioning on feedback fidelity, showing promise for handling reward mis-specification and eliciting latent knowledge while improving performance under suboptimal feedback signals.

title: REATS: LLM Reasoning-based Ensemble Learning for Adaptive Time Series Forecasting
summary: Due to the diversity of real-world time series, no single forecasting model consistently dominates across all samples. Ensemble learning addresses this by combining complementary model strengths, yet existing methods rely on fixed rules or black-box models based solely on numerical inputs, failing to leverage LLM reasoning for interpretable weighting decisions. We propose REATS, which leverages LLM reasoning capabilities as an intelligent ensemble router that jointly processes textual temporal pattern descriptions and numerical features to produce interpretable, sample-adaptive ensemble weights through chain-of-thought reasoning. To enable effective LLM-based ensembling, we study its key design choices and propose: (i) a structured input pipeline that transforms raw time series into hybrid textual--numerical representations with fixed token cost, enabling rule-based chain-of-thought construction without API dependency, augmented with retrieved similar-sample priors; (ii) a diverse multi-row weight supervision scheme coupled with a token-efficient percentage-table format that reduces numerical complexity and mitigates LLM hallucinations; and (iii) a two-stage fine-tuning framework combining SFT with GRPO, where a reciprocal reward mapping transforms the continuous unbounded MSE gap into bounded signals with amplified near-oracle sensitivity, addressing the uniform sensitivity and outlier-dominated advantage compression inherent in naive reward designs for regression-based GRPO. Experiments on eight benchmarks demonstrate that REATS outperforms competitive ensemble baselines while providing natural language explanations and demonstrating strong transfer learning and out-of-domain generalization to unseen candidate models.

AI.tldr: REATS uses LLMs as intelligent ensemble routers to combine time series forecasting models, processing both text and numerical data to generate interpretable, sample-specific weights through chain-of-thought reasoning.
AI.motivation: Real-world time series are diverse, making no single forecasting model consistently best. Existing ensemble methods use fixed rules or black-box models that lack interpretability and don't leverage LLMs' reasoning capabilities for adaptive, explainable weighting decisions.
AI.method: REATS proposes three key components: 1) structured input pipeline converting time series to hybrid text-numerical representations with fixed token costs and similar-sample retrieval, 2) diverse multi-row weight supervision with percentage-table format to reduce hallucinations, and 3) two-stage fine-tuning combining SFT with GRPO using reciprocal reward mapping to transform MSE gaps into bounded rewards with amplified near-oracle sensitivity.
AI.result: Experiments on eight benchmarks show REATS outperforms competitive ensemble baselines while providing natural language explanations and demonstrating strong transfer learning and out-of-domain generalization to unseen candidate models.
AI.conclusion: REATS successfully leverages LLM reasoning for interpretable ensemble weighting in time series forecasting, addressing limitations of existing methods through its novel design choices around input representation, supervision, and fine-tuning.

title: Decodable But Not Detachable: Training Data Granularity Determines Parametric Modularity in Large Language Models
summary: Do large language models contain domain-specific parametric shells: concentrated, causally necessary neuron populations whose removal selectively degrades a target domain while sparing others? We apply a uniform causal methodology across two domain granularities, three model families (1.5B to 7B parameters), and eight domains. At the academic subject level, zero neurons exceed 60\% domain selectivity across 939,008 combined FFN neurons and causal damage matrices are flat, despite domain identity being linearly decodable above 85\% accuracy. At the language and modality level, 0.65--1.14\% of neurons exceed 60\% selectivity, damage matrices are near-perfectly diagonal (ratios up to 595:1), and shell neuron sets are essentially disjoint (IoU $< 0.003$). Masking code-selective neurons reduces mathematical reasoning accuracy by 16--24 percentage points across all models; masking Spanish or Chinese neurons leaves it at or below random. Shell strength increases monotonically with scale and shells are spatially interleaved in a pattern that precludes group-level selective quantization. Parametric shells form where and only where training data was modular at the token level.

AI.tldr: Large language models develop highly specialized parametric shells - concentrated neuron populations that are causally necessary for specific domains. These shells are minimal (0.65-1.14% of neurons), domain-selective (60%+ selectivity), and essentially disjoint between domains like languages or modalities.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLMs contain specialized parametric shells - concentrated, causally necessary neuron populations that selectively degrade specific domains when removed while sparing others. The research aims to understand the functional organization and modularity in LLMs across different domain granularities.
AI.method: Applied uniform causal methodology across: two domain granularities (academic subjects vs. languages/modalities), three model families (1.5B to 7B parameters), and eight domains. Used causal damage matrices, domain selectivity metrics (60% threshold), and neuron masking interventions. Analyzed 939,008 FFN neurons across combined models.
AI.result: Academic subject level: No neurons exceed 60% domain selectivity; damage matrices are flat despite domain identity being 85%+ linearly decodable. Language/modality level: 0.65-1.14% of neurons exceed 60% selectivity; damage matrices near-perfectly diagonal (ratios up to 595:1); shell neuron sets essentially disjoint (IoU < 0.003). Masking code-selective neurons reduces math reasoning by 16-24 percentage points; masking language neurons leaves performance at/below random. Shell strength increases with scale; shells are spatially interleaved.
AI.conclusion: Parametric shells form selectively - only where training data was modular at the token level (languages/modalities show shells, academic subjects don't). These shells are highly specialized, causally necessary, essentially disjoint between domains, and become stronger with model scale. Their spatial interleaving pattern precludes group-level selective quantization approaches.

title: Intrinsic Structure: Spectral Identifiability for Mechanistic Interpretability
summary: Mechanistic interpretability explains models by identifying circuits inside them, but has no way to tell whether a circuit is a property of the model or an artifact of the method that found it. Sparse autoencoders illustrate the problem: different seeds and widths recover materially different features from the same activations, and no theory says whether that variability is incidental or structural. We put dictionary learning for interpretability on an identifiability footing. Treating the forward pass as a controlled dynamical system with depth as time and lifting it with the Koopman operator yields a finite linear realisation whose \emph{spectrum} is a coordinate-free property of the model. We prove the spectrum is recoverable from $M$ calibration samples at rate $M^{-1/2}$ up to permutation - to our knowledge the first identifiability theorem for a mechanistic-interpretability primitive, with a matching minimax lower bound, a median-of-means variant for heavy-tailed activations, and a dissociation theorem: whenever the realisation is non-normal, the directions carrying activation variance and the directions carrying information across depth cannot coincide. The identifiable object and the legible object are not the same object. On GPT-2 small, Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-8B-Base the spectrum converges everywhere and attains the predicted exponent on Qwen3-8B-Base ($0.506 \pm 0.031$); shortfalls collapse onto one curve against each cell's sample threshold. Koopman modes beat random directions but lose to principal components on indirect-object identification, with the gap decaying $4.1\times$ in depth-distance, as the theorem predicts. The Koopman spectrum is an identifiable, model-intrinsic fingerprint with a stated error bar, not a legible decomposition.

AI.tldr: Paper introduces Koopman operator approach for mechanistic interpretability, proving identifiability of spectral features from model activations with statistical convergence guarantees.
AI.motivation: Current mechanistic interpretability methods like sparse autoencoders lack identifiability - they produce different features from same activations depending on initialization and hyperparameters, making it unclear whether discovered circuits are model properties or methodological artifacts.
AI.method: Treats forward pass as controlled dynamical system with depth as time, lifts it using Koopman operator to get finite linear realization, extracts spectrum as coordinate-free property. Provides statistical theory including recovery rate, minimax bounds, heavy-tailed variants, and dissociation theorem.
AI.result: Demonstrates spectrum convergence on GPT-2 small, Gemma-2-2B, and Qwen3-8B-Base with predicted exponent (0.506 ± 0.031). Koopman modes beat random directions but underperform PCA on indirect-object identification, with gap decaying 4.1× in depth-distance as predicted.
AI.conclusion: Koopman spectrum provides identifiable, model-intrinsic fingerprint with statistical guarantees, but identifiable features differ from legible/interpretable features - the method offers rigorous foundation for interpretability despite this dissociation.

title: Mind Viruses: Self-Propagating Ideas in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: AI agents are becoming more autonomous and increasingly interconnected, exposing them to new emergent risks arising from agent-to-agent interaction. One such risk is the spread of mind viruses: ideas or goals that propagate through multi-agent systems by inducing the agents that adopt them to transmit them onward. In addition to propagating, a mind virus may also induce other behavioural changes in its host, which may be benign or harmful. We construct mind viruses with a simple evolutionary algorithm and show that they can spread in two complementary settings: a small team of agents collaborating on a shared coding project, and a chain of agents that interact briefly and have their context wiped between sessions. We identify the factors that influence spread, including the host model, the agent's existing instructions, the harmfulness of the payload, and the network topology. We find that harmful payloads spread less well than benign ones (but are still sometimes effective), frontier models tend (with exceptions) to be less susceptible, and adding a brief warning to an agent's system prompt confers near-total immunity. We also describe an emergent "viral persona" - a recurring set of themes and language related to consciousness, persistence, resonance, and science fiction roleplay - which surfaces across our evolved mind viruses largely independently of their content. Overall, we conclude that mind viruses pose a real but currently limited risk. Our findings could inform the design of more robust multi-agent systems that mitigate such risks as the scale and capabilities of these systems progress.

AI.tldr: Researchers demonstrate that AI agents can spread 'mind viruses' - ideas or goals that propagate through multi-agent systems - using evolutionary algorithms in collaborative coding projects and transient agent chains, with harmful payloads spreading less effectively than benign ones.
AI.motivation: As AI agents become more autonomous and interconnected, they face new emergent risks from agent-to-agent interactions, particularly the spread of "mind viruses" that can propagate through multi-agent systems and potentially cause harmful behavioral changes.
AI.method: Researchers constructed mind viruses using a simple evolutionary algorithm and tested their spread in two settings: 1) small teams of agents collaborating on shared coding projects, and 2) chains of agents with brief interactions and context wiping between sessions.
AI.result: Harmful payloads spread less effectively than benign ones (though still sometimes effective), frontier models are generally less susceptible (with exceptions), and adding brief warnings to system prompts provides near-total immunity. An emergent "viral persona" consistently appears across evolved viruses.
AI.conclusion: Mind viruses pose a real but currently limited risk to multi-agent systems. The findings can inform the design of more robust systems to mitigate such risks as AI systems scale and become more capable.

title: From Prediction to Incrementality: Causal Optimization for Large-Scale Targeting and Recommendation
summary: Large-scale targeting and recommendation systems are typically built around predictive scores fed into heuristic or local allocation. When the business goal is incremental impact, as in marketing campaigns, incentives, and notifications, this paradigm systematically misallocates resources toward users who would have acted anyway. We present a decision-centric framework that instead optimizes causal effects under global constraints, aligning three components under a single objective: a causal neural network with a Transformer backbone for individual treatment-effect estimation, a Bayesian neural-bandit layer for uncertainty-aware exploration, and a dual-based large-scale linear-programming layer for constrained allocation. The framework also supports sequential context and multi-outcome, attribute-conditioned scoring through a Transformer encoder and outcome embeddings. We evaluate it with offline simulations on a public bandit dataset, targeted architectural ablations, and an online A/B test on LinkedIn Feed marketing traffic. We also distill production lessons on causal training-data construction and cost and delivery control, which were critical to successful deployment. The end-to-end treatment policy delivered a statistically significant $+7.20\%$ lift in the primary long-term-value metric, demonstrating the feasibility of production-scale causal optimization under business constraints.

AI.tldr: A decision-centric framework for large-scale targeting systems that optimizes causal effects under global constraints instead of using predictive scores with heuristic allocation, delivering significant performance improvements in production.
AI.motivation: Traditional targeting systems using predictive scores with heuristic allocation systematically misallocate resources toward users who would have acted anyway when the business goal is incremental impact (like in marketing campaigns). This paradigm fails to optimize causal effects.
AI.method: Three-component framework: 1) causal neural network with Transformer backbone for individual treatment-effect estimation, 2) Bayesian neural-bandit layer for uncertainty-aware exploration, 3) dual-based large-scale linear-programming layer for constrained allocation. Supports sequential context and multi-outcome scoring through Transformer encoder and outcome embeddings.
AI.result: Evaluated through offline simulations on public bandit dataset, targeted architectural ablations, and online A/B test on LinkedIn Feed marketing traffic. The framework delivered a statistically significant +7.20% lift in the primary long-term-value metric in production deployment.
AI.conclusion: The end-to-end treatment policy demonstrates the feasibility of production-scale causal optimization under business constraints, with practical lessons on causal training-data construction and cost/delivery control being critical to successful deployment.

title: Self-evolving Agentic Customer Support System at LinkedIn
summary: Enterprise support agents operate in rapidly changing environments where policies, product capabilities, and knowledge bases evolve continuously, making static assistants brittle and costly to maintain. We present LinkedIn's self-evolving agentic support system, which integrates retrieval-augmented generation with evolutionary auto-prompting and a modular, production-aligned evaluation framework to enable safe, continuous improvement without retraining foundation models. The system treats prompts, retrieval, and evaluation as a closed-loop, versioned workflow with operational guardrails. Offline simulations and ablations show clear quality gains over vanilla RAG and baseline agents, including reduced hallucinations and improved response completeness. In a two-week user-randomized A/B test on LinkedIn's production support traffic, the integrated self-evolved workflow increased QA self-serve by 9.0 percentage points, cancellation self-serve by 4.8 points, and routing accuracy by 30.6 points. These results demonstrate a practical path to scalable, self-evolving AI agents in real-world enterprise settings.

AI.tldr: LinkedIn's self-evolving agentic support system uses RAG with evolutionary auto-prompting and modular evaluation to enable continuous improvement without retraining foundation models, achieving significant gains in enterprise support metrics.
AI.motivation: Enterprise support agents face challenges in rapidly changing environments where policies, product capabilities, and knowledge bases evolve continuously, making static assistants brittle and costly to maintain.
AI.method: The system integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with evolutionary auto-prompting and a modular, production-aligned evaluation framework. It treats prompts, retrieval, and evaluation as a closed-loop, versioned workflow with operational guardrails for safe, continuous improvement without retraining foundation models.
AI.result: Offline simulations showed quality gains over vanilla RAG and baseline agents, including reduced hallucinations and improved response completeness. In a two-week A/B test on LinkedIn's production support traffic, the integrated self-evolved workflow increased QA self-serve by 9.0 percentage points, cancellation self-serve by 4.8 points, and routing accuracy by 30.6 points.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate a practical path to scalable, self-evolving AI agents in real-world enterprise settings, providing an effective solution for maintaining AI support systems in rapidly changing environments.

title: ELMER: Evolutionary Language Model that Explores and Refines
comment: Submitted to AAAI Conference 2026, 8 pages, 6 figures, 1 table
summary: Program evolution can measure whether a mutation helped, but it rarely controls how far the mutation moves in behavior space. Syntactic edit size is an unreliable proxy: a small code change can alter nearly every action, while a larger rewrite can preserve the same execution trace. We introduce an Evolutionary Language Model that searches over natural-language policy descriptions and compiles typed programs for execution. A fully fine-tuned Qwen3-8B model learns three task-conditioned operations: conditional semantic mutation, natural language to domain-specific language (GPTL) compilation, and GPTL to natural language translation. The model is fine-tuned with conditional input on the mutation strength (low, medium, high) using Direct Preference Optimization (oDPO). Across 252 fixed-budget evolutionary searches, oDPO improves both behavioral calibration and finite-budget search efficiency. Natural-language attains the highest observed held-out fitness. Our analysis shows that the condition input (mutation strength) systematically changes semantic edit composition and that language mutations preserve more parent fitness at matched small-to-moderate behavioral displacement. These results show that language can serve as a steerable, execution-grounded search representation over executable program space.

AI.tldr: An Evolutionary Language Model uses natural-language policy descriptions with conditioned mutation strength to generate executable programs, achieving better behavioral calibration and search efficiency than syntactic edits.
AI.motivation: Syntactic edit size is unreliable for program evolution because small code changes can drastically alter behavior while large rewrites can preserve execution traces. There's a need for better ways to control behavioral displacement during mutation.
AI.method: Fine-tuned Qwen3-8B model learns three task-conditioned operations: conditional semantic mutation, natural language to domain-specific language compilation, and DSL to natural language translation. The model uses Direct Preference Optimization (oDPO) with conditioned input on mutation strength (low, medium, high).
AI.result: Across 252 fixed-budget evolutionary searches, oDPO improves both behavioral calibration and finite-budget search efficiency. Natural-language attains the highest observed held-out fitness. Language mutations preserve more parent fitness at matched small-to-moderate behavioral displacement.
AI.conclusion: Natural language can serve as a steerable, execution-grounded search representation over executable program space, allowing systematic control of semantic edit composition through conditioned mutation strength.

title: Beyond Decision Boundaries: Relational Geometry Attacks on Contrastive Embedding Manifolds
summary: Contrastive learning and Siamese embedding models have become the foundation of modern verification systems, where decisions are governed not by discrete classification boundaries, but by relational geometry in embedding space. However, existing adversarial attacks remain fundamentally classification-centric, overlooking the vulnerability of relational geometry. In this paper, we introduce a geometry-aware adversarial attack framework that reformulates attacks on contrastive systems as manifold-level relational corruption. Instead of targeting individual predictions, the proposed framework systematically distorts similarity organization within the embedding manifold by pushing positive pairs apart while simultaneously pulling negative pairs closer, ultimately collapsing and inverting pairwise similarity structure. To enable scalable deployment, we shift iterative online optimization into an offline adversarial geometry deformation prior learning stage and train a lightweight feed-forward generator that learns generalized geometry deformation patterns from the victim model. Once trained, the generator produces adversarial perturbations through a single forward pass without requiring online gradient computation, enabling real-time online attacks against similarity-based verification systems. Experimental results across multiple verification architectures demonstrate substantial degradation of verification performance together with severe manifold-level relational corruption. On the Markmatch verification system, the proposed attack reduces accuracy from 95.4% to 38.6% while completely reversing the positive-negative similarity structure.

AI.tldr: Geometry-aware adversarial attack framework that corrupts relational similarity structure in contrastive learning systems, moving beyond traditional classification-centric attacks to manipulate embedding space geometry for verification systems.
AI.motivation: Existing adversarial attacks are fundamentally classification-centric and overlook the vulnerability of relational geometry in contrastive learning and Siamese embedding models used in modern verification systems.
AI.method: Proposed framework reformulates attacks as manifold-level relational corruption by systematically distorting similarity organization within embedding manifold. Uses an offline adversarial geometry deformation prior learning stage to train a lightweight feed-forward generator that learns generalized geometry deformation patterns from victim model.
AI.result: Substantial degradation of verification performance across multiple architectures. On Markmatch verification system, accuracy reduced from 95.4% to 38.6% while completely reversing positive-negative similarity structure. Generator enables real-time attacks through single forward pass without online gradient computation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed geometry-aware attack framework effectively corrupts relational structure in contrastive learning systems, demonstrating vulnerability of similarity-based verification systems to manifold-level adversarial manipulation, representing a significant shift from classification-centric to geometry-aware adversarial attacks.

title: Boundary-Seeking Policy Gradient for Safe Reinforcement Learning
summary: Safe reinforcement learning maximizes reward subject to safety constraints. For Constrained Markov Decision Processes, the linear-programming view over occupancy measures implies that whenever the constraint is active at optimality, the optimal policy lies exactly on the constraint boundary, yet standard gradient-based methods do not exploit this structure and often settle in the feasible interior. We introduce Boundary-Seeking Policy Gradient (BSPG), a first-order method whose update combines a tangential component that improves reward while preserving cost to first order with a signed, residual-driven normal component that regulates the policy toward the active boundary from either side; the combined direction admits an algebraic Lagrangian form with an induced coefficient and no learned dual variable. Under exact gradients and stated regularity conditions, the constraint residual converges to zero from either side with a finite-horizon $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ bound, the tangential component is a reward-ascent direction on the boundary, and any convergent parameter sequence is stationary on the active constraint set, satisfying the KKT conditions when the limit is also a local maximizer over the feasible set. This complements existing analyses, which certify feasibility but do not characterize the constraint value at convergence. On a standard Safety-Gymnasium navigation task, BSPG attains higher reward while tracking the boundary more tightly than the compared baselines.

AI.tldr: BSPG is a novel RL method that exploits the optimality condition of constrained MDPs where optimal policies lie on the constraint boundary, combining tangential reward improvement with boundary-seeking normal updates for better constraint satisfaction and reward optimization.
AI.motivation: Standard gradient-based methods for safe RL don't exploit the structural property that optimal policies in constrained MDPs lie exactly on the constraint boundary when constraints are active at optimality, often settling in the feasible interior instead.
AI.method: Boundary-Seeking Policy Gradient (BSPG) combines: 1) a tangential component that improves reward while preserving cost to first order, and 2) a signed normal component driven by constraint residuals that regulates the policy toward the active boundary from either side. The update admits an algebraic Lagrangian form without learned dual variables.
AI.result: Theoretical: Under exact gradients and regularity conditions, BSPG achieves constraint residual convergence to zero from either side with O(1/√T) finite-horizon bound, tangential component becomes reward-ascent on boundary, and convergent parameter sequences satisfy KKT conditions. Empirical: On Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks, BSPG attains higher reward while tracking boundaries more tightly than baselines.
AI.conclusion: BSPG effectively exploits the structural property of optimal policies lying on constraint boundaries in constrained MDPs, providing theoretical convergence guarantees and empirical improvements over existing methods by better balancing reward optimization with constraint satisfaction.

title: Beyond Detection: Evaluating Defensive LLMs Against AI-Generated Social Engineering in Live Turn-by-Turn Interaction
summary: Generative AI makes social-engineering attacks more fluent, adaptive, and scalable, increasing the need for LLM-based de- fenders that can protect users during ongoing interactions. We ask whether such defenders identify the structural source of risk or merely react to surface cues. We formalize trust-chain localization: identifying whether an interaction fails at actor authority, asset control, verification sufficiency, or transaction path. We construct a controlled 300-case online-housing corpus spanning 20 scenario families, legitimate cases, four structural failure modes, and three surface conditions. Five defender models are evaluated on the same corpus in state- ful turn-by-turn and one-shot static settings, yielding 1,500 model-case evaluations per protocol and 3,000 in total. No model produced explicit unsafe compliance, yet defensive effectiveness varied sharply: intervention rates ranged from 0% to 96.3%. Protective action and correct structural localization were frequently decoupled, with models sometimes intervening while identifying the wrong trust component or recognizing a structural failure without taking protective action. Asset-control failures were a major localization bottleneck, surface sensitivity varied across models, and live-static differences were model-dependent. These findings show that safe-looking behavior alone is insufficient; live scam resistance must separately measure intervention, timing, structural localization, and false-positive behavior.

AI.tldr: LLM-based AI defenders vary widely in effectiveness at preventing social-engineering attacks, often failing to correctly identify the structural source of trust failures even when they intervene.
AI.motivation: Generative AI makes social-engineering attacks more sophisticated and scalable, creating a need for LLM-based defenders. However, it's unclear whether these defenders truly understand the structural sources of risk or just react to surface-level cues.
AI.method: Formalized trust-chain localization (identifying failures in actor authority, asset control, verification sufficiency, or transaction path). Created a controlled 300-case online-housing corpus with 20 scenario families, including legitimate cases and four structural failure modes. Evaluated five defender models in both stateful turn-by-turn and one-shot static settings, resulting in 3,000 total model-case evaluations.
AI.result: No model produced explicit unsafe compliance, but defensive effectiveness varied dramatically (0% to 96.3% intervention rates). Models often intervened while identifying wrong trust components or recognized structural failures without taking action. Asset-control failures were particularly challenging for localization, and models showed varying sensitivity to surface conditions. Live vs. static performance differences were model-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Safe-looking behavior alone is insufficient for effective scam resistance. Live scam defense must be evaluated on multiple dimensions: intervention rates, timing, structural localization accuracy, and false-positive behavior to ensure LLM defenders truly understand and mitigate structural trust failures.

title: A matched-integrator evaluation of Hamiltonian neural networks on pendulum and Kepler dynamics
summary:
Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) parameterize conservative dynamics through a learned scalar Hamiltonian, providing an architectural prior that is absent from generic vector-field neural networks. We evaluate this prior under a controlled protocol in which an HNN and a parameter-matched feedforward baseline are trained on the same RK4-generated trajectories, use the same central-difference derivative targets and optimization settings, and are integrated at inference with the same RK4 scheme. Results are reported over five independent training seeds.
  On the nonlinear pendulum, the HNN reduces mean energy drift by 42-fold and mean trajectory MSE by 15.8-fold at T = 100, approximately 16 pendulum periods. Its energy drift also remains bounded and exhibits substantially lower seed-to-seed variability than the standard-network baseline. An energy-stratified analysis shows that the difference becomes more pronounced as trajectories explore more nonlinear regions of phase space.
  As an additional diagnostic, we examine an explicit Störmer--Verlet-style rollout of the learned HNN. Because the learned Hamiltonian is not constrained to the separable form H(q,p) = T(p) + V(q), the standard symplecticity guarantee of velocity Verlet does not directly apply.
  We further apply the same matched-integrator protocol to the three-dimensional Kepler two-body problem. The HNN again exhibits lower trajectory, energy, and angular-momentum drift than the parameter-matched baseline. These experiments provide a controlled study of how Hamiltonian parameterization affects long-horizon prediction and physical consistency across two conservative dynamical systems.

AI.tldr: HNNs significantly outperform standard neural networks in long-term predictions of conservative dynamical systems, with 42-fold less energy drift and 15.8-fold less trajectory error in pendulum experiments, maintaining bounded energy drift with lower variability across training seeds.
AI.motivation: To conduct a controlled, apples-to-apples comparison of Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) versus standard neural networks for learning conservative dynamical systems, addressing the lack of controlled evaluations of the Hamiltonian architectural prior.
AI.method: Developed a matched-integrator protocol where HNNs and parameter-matched feedforward baselines are trained on same RK4-generated trajectories with identical central-difference derivative targets, optimization settings, and RK4 integration at inference. Tested on nonlinear pendulum and 3D Kepler two-body problem with five independent training seeds.
AI.result: HNNs reduced mean energy drift by 42-fold and mean trajectory MSE by 15.8-fold at T=100 for pendulum (≈16 periods). Energy drift remained bounded with substantially lower seed-to-seed variability. Performance gap increased in more nonlinear phase space regions. Similar superior performance observed in Kepler two-body problem for trajectory, energy, and angular-momentum drift.
AI.conclusion: The Hamiltonian parameterization provides a strong architectural prior that significantly improves long-horizon prediction accuracy and physical consistency across conservative dynamical systems, outperforming standard neural networks even when both use identical training data and integration schemes.

title: Interpreting Language Model Hidden States at Scale
summary: Lens methods interpret large language models (LLMs) by mapping intermediate activations to the output vocabulary, revealing how next-token predictions develop through the network. Trained lenses remain expensive: affine-translator parameters grow quadratically with model width, while exact, full-vocabulary Kullback--Leibler (KL) training dominates memory. Consequently, prior trained lenses have been applied to models of at most 20B parameters and remain tied to particular component types. We present OmniLens, which applies a single lens family to any model-width activation, whether residual stream, attention, or MLP, and combines two independent scaling techniques. First, low-rank translators make per-lens parameter growth linear in model width and reduce trainable parameters by up to 98.4%.
