Second, Subset-KL materializes only selected vocabulary logits: its Top-k mode cuts peak training memory by up to 70%, while its importance-sampled variant retains unbiased stochastic gradients for the full KL. These savings enable a dense ensemble of 482 lenses for LLaMA-3.3-70B, providing 6x the coverage of a residual-stream design at the same depth. Model-wide coverage then reveals what single-component lenses cannot: the components where a behavior is most visible need not be those where intervention is most effective, and the most effective interventions lie outside the attention heads examined by prior lens studies. Across three case studies (prompt-injection detection, multi-hop memory injection, and toxicity localization), OmniLens reproduces key published results at substantially lower cost.

AI.tldr: OmniLens is a scalable lens method that can interpret any model-width activation in LLMs with low-rank translators and Subset-KL training, enabling efficient analysis of large models like LLaMA-3.3-70B.
AI.motivation: Existing lens methods for interpreting LLMs have scalability limitations: they require expensive affine translators that grow quadratically with model width, and full-vocabulary KL training dominates memory. This limits their application to models up to 20B parameters and ties them to specific component types.
AI.method: OmniLens introduces two scaling techniques: 1) Low-rank translators that reduce per-lens parameter growth from quadratic to linear in model width, reducing trainable parameters by up to 98.4%. 2) Subset-KL training that materializes only selected vocabulary logits - with Top-k mode cutting training memory by up to 70%, and importance-sampled variant maintaining unbiased stochastic gradients for full KL.
AI.result: OmniLens enables dense ensemble of 482 lenses for LLaMA-3.3-70B, providing 6x coverage of residual-stream design at same depth. It reveals novel insights: components where behaviors are most visible aren't necessarily where interventions are most effective, and most effective interventions lie outside attention heads examined by prior studies. Successfully reproduces key published results in prompt-injection detection, multi-hop memory injection, and toxicity localization at substantially lower cost.
AI.conclusion: OmniLens provides a scalable, universal lens framework that overcomes previous limitations in interpreting large LLMs, enabling comprehensive model-wide analysis and revealing previously inaccessible insights about component behavior and intervention effectiveness.

title: STCAD: Scalable Trajectory Clustering and Anomaly Detection on Terabyte-Scale AIS Data
summary: We present a scalable framework for unsupervised clustering of maritime trajectories derived from terabyte-scale Automatic Identification System (AIS) archives. Variable-length trajectories are encoded with a custom BERT-based model trained via masked token modeling and clustered using CURE hierarchical clustering, producing physically interpretable trajectory groups without requiring a predefined number of clusters. An intrinsic unsupervised anomaly detection method based on reconstruction loss and clustering noise assignment identifies irregular navigation patterns. The framework is demonstrated on a national-scale AIS dataset comprising billions of messages spanning one year, yielding stable trajectory clusters and a clear separation between nominal and anomalous vessel behavior.

AI.tldr: A scalable unsupervised framework for clustering maritime AIS trajectories using BERT-based encoding and hierarchical clustering, with anomaly detection via reconstruction loss.
AI.motivation: There is a need to analyze massive-scale maritime trajectory data from AIS systems (terabyte-scale archives with billions of messages) to identify patterns and anomalies in vessel behavior without supervision or predefined cluster numbers.
AI.method: Variable-length AIS trajectories are encoded using a custom BERT-based model trained with masked token modeling. CURE hierarchical clustering is applied to these encodings to produce physically interpretable trajectory groups without requiring predefined cluster numbers. An intrinsic unsupervised anomaly detection method uses reconstruction loss from the BERT model and clustering noise assignment.
AI.result: The framework was demonstrated on a national-scale AIS dataset spanning one year with billions of messages, producing stable trajectory clusters and achieving clear separation between nominal and anomalous vessel behavior.
AI.conclusion: The proposed scalable framework successfully enables unsupervised clustering and anomaly detection in massive maritime trajectory datasets, providing physically interpretable results without supervision requirements.

title: Logit-Boundary Geometric Belief Interfaces and Sparse Sheaf-Enclave Protocols: A Self-Contained Substrate for Secure Network Electronic Health Record (EHR) Interoperability
comment: 39 pages; executable Julia verification code included as ancillary material; companion public benchmark: https://github.com/AlvinSpivey/GBI-BoundaryBench
summary: Electronic health-record interoperability is a boundary problem: legacy systems, generative models, terminology services, identity systems, and human reviewers may each expose rich internal states, while operational exchange requires a narrow shared interface of typed claims, bounded uncertainty, provenance, and explicit admission or abstention. This paper details a mathematical and engineering architecture for that interface. The organizing idea is the logit boundary: a discovery model may propose pre-threshold scores over a local categorical decision, but a deterministic judgment substrate decides whether the proposal is admissible, requires review, or must be quarantined before any Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) transaction is constructed. The resulting Geometric Belief Interface (GBI) combines finite boundary semantics, local Dirichlet evidence, cellular-sheaf and mapping-cone diagnostics, advisory geometric audit charts, and a Decentralized Cryptographic Sheaf-Enclave (DCSE) protocol sketch for fail-closed deployment. The framework does not establish clinical truth, global representation alignment, or end-to-end safety; it defines certificate-producing checks at a model-to-system boundary. A companion frozen synthetic benchmark, GBI BoundaryBench v0.1, evaluated Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on 256 held-out tasks across three evidence modes (768 canonical executions). All executions completed, but none produced an output accepted by the benchmark contract: 369 were rejected during safe parsing and 399 during schema validation, yielding zero coverage and deterministic quarantine. This empirical result is deliberately narrow - one 4B open-weight model under one frozen interface - and is reported as evidence about the admission boundary, not as a general claim about LLM capability or clinical safety. A Julia appendix verifies numerical certificates using standard libraries.

AI.tldr: A mathematical framework called Geometric Belief Interface (GBI) defines a logit boundary between clinical AI models and healthcare systems, requiring deterministic validation of model proposals before FHIR transactions can proceed, with initial testing showing complete rejection of a 4B-parameter model's outputs.
AI.motivation: Electronic health-record interoperability requires a narrow shared interface between complex legacy systems, AI models, and human reviewers, addressing the boundary problem where rich internal states must be reduced to verifiable, bounded claims for safe operational exchange.
AI.method: Proposes a Geometric Belief Interface (GBI) architecture using a logit boundary concept where discovery models propose pre-threshold scores, and a deterministic substrate decides admissibility. Combines finite boundary semantics, local Dirichlet evidence, cellular-sheaf diagnostics, geometric audit charts, and a decentralized cryptographic protocol for fail-closed deployment.
AI.result: Benchmark evaluation of Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on 256 tasks across three evidence modes (768 executions) resulted in 100% rejection: 369 during safe parsing and 399 during schema validation, yielding zero coverage and deterministic quarantine. This demonstrates the strict boundary enforcement but is not a general claim about LLM capability.
AI.conclusion: The GBI framework provides certificate-producing boundary checks for model-to-system interfaces without establishing clinical truth or global safety. Initial results show the boundary can be strictly enforced to reject all uncertain proposals, serving as evidence about admission boundaries rather than general AI capability assessments.

title: CRHT: A Continuous Regression Hybrid Transformer for Vessel Trajectory Prediction with Online Cluster Sampling
summary: Accurate vessel trajectory prediction is critical for maritime safety and anomaly detection, yet existing models often struggle with geographic bias and navigational realism. We propose the Continuous Regression Hybrid Transformer (CRHT), a deep learning framework designed to forecast vessel motion using Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. To mitigate spatial data imbalance, we introduce an online K-means cluster sampling strategy that ensures diverse exposure to rare maneuvers during training. Our hybrid architecture integrates 1D convolutional layers for local kinematic feature extraction with a multi-head attention mechanism for global temporal context. CRHT demonstrates superior performance in short-term forecasting, achieving the lowest errors at the 1-hour horizon. The results demonstrate that while discrete models provide high navigational stability over long horizons, CRHT offers an optimal balance of precision and maneuver tracking for real-time maritime surveillance.

AI.tldr: CRHT is a Continuous Regression Hybrid Transformer for vessel trajectory prediction that combines 1D CNNs for local features with multi-head attention for global context, achieving best short-term accuracy with 1-hour horizon predictions.
AI.motivation: Existing vessel trajectory prediction models suffer from geographic bias and lack navigational realism, which is problematic for maritime safety and anomaly detection applications.
AI.method: CRHT framework uses AIS data with: 1) Online K-means cluster sampling strategy to mitigate spatial data imbalance and ensure exposure to rare maneuvers; 2) Hybrid architecture integrating 1D convolutional layers for local kinematic feature extraction with multi-head attention mechanism for global temporal context.
AI.result: CRHT demonstrates superior performance in short-term forecasting, achieving the lowest errors at the 1-hour horizon. Discrete models provide better navigational stability over long horizons, but CRHT offers optimal balance of precision and maneuver tracking for real-time surveillance.
AI.conclusion: CRHT represents an effective deep learning solution for vessel trajectory prediction that addresses geographic bias through innovative sampling, and combines local feature extraction with global context modeling for optimal real-time maritime surveillance applications.

title: Neuroevolution Arena: Nested Ecological Evaluation of Update-and-Inheritance Regimes across Neural Architectures
summary: Competitive artificial-life systems can rank trained controllers differently under training and ecological evaluation. We present Neuroevolution Arena, a GPU-accelerated spatial ecology of independently parameterized neural-network cells, and an audit-tracked nested evaluation protocol. Three implementation-specific update-and-inheritance regimes (EvoEvo, EvoRL, and RLRL) are crossed with two neural architectures for 50,000 generations in three independent training runs per condition. One saved elite-controller artifact from each of the 18 runs enters an aligned-run frozen-evaluation design comprising 198 computational jobs. Pairwise effects average three seed-defined ecological contexts (two cooperation-permitting and one attack-permitting) within each aligned training-run block; the independent level remains n = 3 runs per condition. RL-enabled regimes attain higher recorded training fitness than EvoEvo, whereas pairwise outcomes show architecture-conditioned majority patterns and substantial artifact dependence. Six-way winners vary across artifacts and contexts, and the prespecified survival endpoint has a complete floor. We contribute a nested protocol that separates training-run artifacts from evaluation contexts and exposes, rather than conceals, their different sources of variation.

AI.tldr: Neuroevolution Arena introduces a GPU-accelerated competitive artificial-life system with audit-tracked nested evaluation to separate training artifacts from ecological evaluation contexts, revealing substantial variation in controller rankings between training and testing.
AI.motivation: Competitive artificial-life systems often rank trained controllers differently during training versus ecological evaluation, creating a need for evaluation protocols that separate training artifacts from testing contexts and expose different sources of variation.
AI.method: Developed Neuroevolution Arena: a GPU-accelerated spatial ecology of neural-network cells with audit-tracked nested evaluation. Tested three update regimes (EvoEvo, EvoRL, RLRL) crossed with two neural architectures over 50,000 generations. Used aligned-run frozen-evaluation design with 198 computational jobs and pairwise effects across three ecological contexts (two cooperation-permitting, one attack-permitting).
AI.result: RL-enabled regimes achieved higher training fitness than EvoEvo. Pairwise outcomes showed architecture-conditioned majority patterns and substantial artifact dependence. Six-way winners varied across artifacts and contexts, and the prespecified survival endpoint had complete floor effects.
AI.conclusion: The nested protocol successfully separates training-run artifacts from evaluation contexts and exposes rather than conceals different sources of variation, providing a valuable framework for evaluating competitive artificial-life systems where controller rankings differ between training and ecological contexts.

title: Toward Human Rights Benchmarking for LLMs: A Pilot Methodology
comment: Best paper, honorable mention, at the ICML 2026 Workshop on AI4Law, Seoul, South Korea
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate legal determinations over what human rights are realized, and how. Yet, no evaluation benchmark exists to assess whether they can reason correctly about human rights law. To this end, we report our efforts to develop a robust and scalable methodology for creating HumRightsBench: the first expert-validated, scenario-based benchmark for evaluating reasoning grounded in the obligation structure of international human rights law. We adapt the IRAC framework for legal reasoning to better suit the unique reasoning patterns of human rights work (substituting P, "proposing remedies," for C, "legal conclusion," yielding IRAP) to structure our evaluation heuristics. We also produce a pilot series of authentic scenarios designed to implicate the many dimensions of real-world human rights issues and annotated by human rights lawyers and professionals across the world. Ultimately, we find that model accuracy scores range considerably across legal reasoning tasks (overall model performance ranges from 0.339 to 0.577, task min-max ranges from 0.025 to 0.774), which strongly implies that HumRightsBench is a capable instrument for advancing this emerging subfield of AI evaluations science at a critical moment in its evolution.

AI.tldr: Researchers developed HumRightsBench, the first expert-validated benchmark for evaluating LLMs' ability to reason about human rights law, adapting legal reasoning frameworks and creating authentic scenarios with professional annotations.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly mediating legal determinations about human rights, but there was no benchmark to assess whether they can reason correctly about human rights law, creating a critical gap in AI evaluation science.
AI.method: Adapted the IRAC legal reasoning framework to IRAP (substituting "Proposing remedies" for "Conclusion") for human rights work, created authentic scenarios designed to implicate real-world human rights issues, and had them annotated by human rights lawyers and professionals worldwide.
AI.result: Model accuracy scores ranged considerably across legal reasoning tasks (overall performance 0.339-0.577, task-specific ranges 0.025-0.774), showing HumRightsBench effectively discriminates model capabilities and identifies reasoning gaps.
AI.conclusion: HumRightsBench is a capable instrument for advancing AI evaluations in human rights law at a critical moment, demonstrating both the need for and viability of expert-validated benchmarks in this emerging subfield.

title: Toward a Theory of Value in AI Alignment
summary: Can AI systems be aligned to human values? The popularization of large language models (LLMs) and multi-modal foundation models has seen a rise in harms spanning from toxic speech and hallucinations to AI agents executing unauthorized actions. Within the field of AI safety, these harmful instances are often framed as the alignment problem, or of models being misaligned with human values. Researchers have responded by pursuing applied and theoretical AI value alignment efforts, often without specifying what they mean by human values. How does the field of AI value alignment conceive of human values? How are these conceptions of values technically operationalized and evaluated? What does the emergent theory of value from this field signify for the future of AI? We annotated 94 value alignment research papers to discern their implicit theory of values in AI. The majority do not define values, relying heavily on preferences as a stand in that runs the risk of reducing complex culturally situated concepts down to binary choices. As researchers dispense with using human annotators for model training and evaluation, turning instead to synthetic data and autorater approaches to aligning and evaluating models, we identify the potential to close off alternative methods for contesting and enacting values in foundation models. In making AI value alignments philosophical commitments explicit, we seek to bring great specificity and under explored perspectives in the debate on whether and how AI can address human values.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques how AI value alignment research conceptualizes human values, finding most papers use preferences as a proxy without defining values, risking reduction of complex cultural concepts to binary choices.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to critically examine how AI safety/alignment research conceptualizes human values, as the field responds to AI harms but often lacks clear definitions of what "human values" mean in this context.
AI.method: The researchers conducted an annotation study of 94 value alignment research papers to discern their implicit theories of values in AI and analyze how these conceptions are technically operationalized and evaluated.
AI.result: The majority of papers do not define values, relying heavily on preferences as a substitute. This approach risks reducing complex culturally situated concepts to binary choices. Researchers are also shifting from human annotators to synthetic data and autorater approaches, potentially closing off alternative methods for contesting and enacting values.
AI.conclusion: By making AI value alignment's philosophical commitments explicit, the paper aims to bring greater specificity and under-explored perspectives to the debate on whether and how AI can address human values, highlighting the limitations of current approaches.

title: Power law graph attention: exact generalization of scaled dot-product attention, empirical collapse at inference
summary: The Large Language Model from Power Law Decoder Representations (PLDR-LLM) and its attention, Power Law Graph Attention (PLGA), replace the fixed bilinear form of scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) with a learned, input-generated bilinear operator $G_{LM}$, built from a positive tensor $A_{LM}$ by elementwise power laws. The architecture is fully specified, verified against pinned reference releases; claims are labeled theorem, conditional theorem, measurement, or conjecture. Unconditionally: PLGA contains SDPA exactly at $G_{LM}=I$; $A_{LM}$ and $A_P$ are strictly entrywise positive, with Perron-Frobenius structure on $A_{LM}$; the DAG regularizer has the NOTEARS walk-counting form and positivity obstructs exact acyclicity; and, under nonresonance (satisfied by standard rotary frequencies), a commutant criterion identifies which operators preserve relative-position dependence. An inference-collapse theorem: exact input invariance of deductive outputs collapses inference to generalized SDPA with a constant operator. Measured invariance: relative fluctuations of $10^{-6}$ and below; perturbation bounds quantify but do not certify cached inference; the assembled proxy misses the decoding margin. A conditional three-stage mechanism (rotary twirl, concentration, row-map contraction) is measured on a released checkpoint. Blockwise training and scoring under the global Gram are stated with explicit target exposure; on tested samples, block and sequential scoring select identical answers and agree on the published TruthfulQA probability-mass metric within $5\times 10^{-5}$ per item. Self-organized criticality enters as a phenomenological framework with an intrinsic order parameter; open claims become falsifiable conjectures. Selected proof cores are machine-checked in Lean 4.

AI.tldr: PLDR-LLM introduces Power Law Graph Attention (PLGA) which replaces SDPA with a learned bilinear operator using elementwise power laws from positive tensors, featuring mathematical guarantees and measured invariance properties.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to replace the fixed bilinear form of standard scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) with a more flexible, learned bilinear operator that can adapt to inputs while maintaining mathematical guarantees and structural properties.
AI.method: Uses Power Law Graph Attention (PLGA) built from positive tensor A_LM via elementwise power laws, includes DAG regularizer, mathematical verification via theorems/conditional theorems, measurement protocols, machine-checked proofs in Lean 4, and blockwise training/scoring under global Gram.
AI.result: PLGA contains SDPA exactly at identity, maintains Perron-Frobenius structure, shows inference-collapse theorem for exact input invariance, measures relative fluctuations below 10^{-6}, achieves near-identical block/sequential scoring on TruthfulQA (within 5×10^{-5} per item), and validates conditional three-stage mechanism on released checkpoint.
AI.conclusion: The PLDR-LLM architecture provides mathematically grounded alternatives to SDPA with learned bilinear operators, maintaining structural guarantees while enabling measurable invariance properties, though some claims remain as falsifiable conjectures within a self-organized criticality framework.

title: Hierarchical Compositionality for An Assistive AI Agent
comment: 25 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://tianyi-fu.github.io/HCAA
summary: AI agents are increasingly being developed to assist humans in various applications, and Large Language Models and other deep network architectures are considered to be state of the art for such agents. These methods are impressive stochastic predictors, but they are resource-hungry, opaque, and known to make arbitrary decisions in novel situations due to the narrow set of underlying representation and processing choices. Our work seeks to explore the design of architectures for such AI agents based on core principles that can be traced back to the early pioneers of AI but are not fully utilized in modern AI methods. We do so in this paper in the context of the core problem of AI agents addressing ambiguity in the objects being referred to by the human participants. Humans address such ambiguity by heuristically leveraging compositional knowledge of domain context and the preferences of the other human participants. Drawing inspiration from this observation, we describe an architecture that embeds the principle of hierarchical compositionality and uses simple heuristics to achieve the desired disambiguation. Specifically, domain objects are represented in terms of primitive attributes drawn from human-validated semantic feature norms, and a hierarchical combination of attributes and concepts automatically identified from a limited observed history of interactions of an assistive agent with specific users. The assistive agent then achieves the desired disambiguation by reasoning with knowledge of this compositional hierarchy; axioms governing domain dynamics; and models of semantic compatibility, session salience, and user-specific thematic preference, requesting human clarification when necessary. Experiments show that our approach consistently outperforms state of the art data-driven baselines, supporting adaptation to specific user profiles.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a compositional hierarchical architecture for AI agents that leverages semantic feature norms and user interaction history to resolve referential ambiguity, outperforming data-driven baselines.
AI.motivation: Current AI agents based on Large Language Models and deep networks are resource-intensive, opaque, and make arbitrary decisions in novel situations due to narrow representations. The paper aims to develop more principled architectures for AI agents that can better handle referential ambiguity, inspired by how humans use compositional domain knowledge and user preferences.
AI.method: The architecture embeds hierarchical compositionality principles, representing domain objects using primitive attributes from human-validated semantic feature norms. It builds hierarchical combinations of attributes and concepts from limited interaction history with specific users. Disambiguation is achieved by reasoning with: compositional hierarchy, domain dynamics axioms, semantic compatibility models, session salience, and user-specific thematic preferences, requesting clarification when needed.
AI.result: Experiments show the approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art data-driven baselines and supports adaptation to specific user profiles.
AI.conclusion: The proposed compositional architecture based on early AI principles provides a more effective and interpretable alternative to current data-driven methods for AI agents dealing with referential ambiguity, with better performance and user adaptation capabilities.

title: MERA: Model Evolution and Routing with Skill Adaptation for Agentic Systems at Scale
summary: LLM agents execute heterogeneous sequences of model calls within a single task: some invocations require careful reasoning, while others are structured steps such as formatting or tool-argument construction. Prior routing methods exploit this asymmetry by assigning easy invocations to a cheaper small model and difficult ones to a large model. Such policies reduce inference cost, but they leave the small model's capability unchanged, so attainable savings remain bounded by the work the student can already solve. MERA instead improves the small model itself, using a single model invocation as the unit of adaptation. In each cycle, MERA replays failed student invocations to obtain execution-verified teacher demonstrations, distills recurring procedures into an iteratively updated SkillBook, and fine-tunes a student LoRA adapter via supervised learning and optional GRPO. Routing serves as supporting machinery for deployment: the improved student is served behind a cost-calibrated router with verifier-backed fallback, and a candidate SkillBook, adapter, or router is admitted only when joint replay preserves task quality. Empirically, four-cycle adaptation raises Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B from 28.7% to 49.7% pass on held-out HumanEval+MBPP. Under verifier-backed fallback, the deployed policy retains 88.3% pass at 60.8% of always-Luna cost. On TAU-2, a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-2B improves from 14/35 to 18/35 and matches an unadapted 4B model. These results indicate that verifier-backed multi-cycle adaptation can increase small-model capability, rather than only routing around a fixed student.

AI.tldr: MERA is a multi-cycle adaptation system that improves small LLMs for agentic tasks by learning from failed executions, distilling recurring procedures into a SkillBook, and fine-tuning the student model, then deploying it with cost-aware routing and verifier-backed fallback.
AI.motivation: Traditional routing methods for LLM agents assign easy tasks to cheap small models and hard tasks to expensive large models, but this approach is limited because the small model's capability remains unchanged. MERA aims to fundamentally improve the small model itself to achieve greater cost savings while maintaining task quality.
AI.method: MERA uses a multi-cycle adaptation approach where: 1) Failed student invocations are replayed to get execution-verified teacher demonstrations, 2) Recurring procedures are distilled into an iteratively updated SkillBook, 3) The student model is fine-tuned using supervised learning and optional GRPO, and 4) Improved student models are deployed with cost-calibrated routing and verifier-backed fallback mechanisms.
AI.result: Four-cycle adaptation improved Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B from 28.7% to 49.7% pass rate on HumanEval+MBPP benchmarks. With verifier-backed fallback, the deployed system maintained 88.3% pass rate at 60.8% of the cost of always using the larger model. On TAU-2, a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-2B improved from 14/35 to 18/35 and matched an unadapted 4B model.
AI.conclusion: MERA demonstrates that verifier-backed multi-cycle adaptation can meaningfully increase small-model capability rather than merely routing around a fixed student, enabling significant cost savings while maintaining or improving performance on complex tasks.

title: Nutrition Data Infrastructure for the AI Era: Operationalizing FAIR for Agent-Mediated Research
summary: AI agents can accelerate nutrition research, but their analyses inherit the identity, semantic, and release ambiguities of the underlying data. We present Nutrition Data Service (NDS), source-preserving infrastructure that operationalizes FAIR for automated use: description resolution makes release-specific records findable; typed crosswalks connect independently released resources; machine-readable interfaces expose versioned sources and crosswalks, making analyses by AI agents replayable and auditable. On food-description benchmarks, NDS shows strong held-out accuracy and outperforms the best published language-model result on NutriBench. External and blinded crosswalk evaluations show that its typed contract favors defensible links and rejects unsupported mappings. In a person-level glycemic-index analysis, pinned NDS inputs produce identical outputs across models and repeated runs, while open-web reconstruction remains unstable. The central result is that agent-mediated nutrition research requires a new data infrastructure for data identity, search, and crosswalk.

AI.tldr: NDS (Nutrition Data Service) is a source-preserving infrastructure that applies FAIR principles for automated AI analysis, addressing data identity and crosswalk challenges in nutrition research.
AI.motivation: AI agents can accelerate nutrition research but face significant challenges with data ambiguities: identity ambiguities (which version of data), semantic ambiguities (meaning differences), and release ambiguities (which release of resources). These ambiguities inherit into AI analyses, making them unreliable and difficult to audit.
AI.method: The authors developed NDS (Nutrition Data Service) as source-preserving infrastructure that operationalizes FAIR principles for automated use. Key features include: 1) description resolution for findable release-specific records, 2) typed crosswalks to connect independently released resources with semantic contracts, and 3) machine-readable interfaces exposing versioned sources and crosswalks.
AI.result: 1) On food-description benchmarks, NDS shows strong held-out accuracy and outperforms best published language-model results on NutriBench. 2) Crosswalk evaluations show typed contracts favor defensible links and reject unsupported mappings. 3) Person-level glycemic-index analysis demonstrates pinned NDS inputs produce identical outputs across models/runs, while open-web reconstruction remains unstable.
AI.conclusion: Agent-mediated nutrition research requires new data infrastructure addressing data identity, search, and crosswalk challenges. NDS provides a solution with source-preserving, FAIR-compliant infrastructure that enables replayable, auditable AI analyses through proper data versioning and typed semantic mappings.

title: Accelerated Learning of High Dimensional Functions with a Tensor-Featured Training Network
summary: In this work we present a method to accelerate the optimization of learning high dimensional functions using deep neural network (DNN). This optimization procedure introduces contextual features into the first layer of a DNN. The parameters of DNN are optimized via standard gradient descent while keeping the input-feature basis fixed. After optimization of the DNN parameters, the feature layer is provided a chance to update and change before DNN optimization resumes. The feature layer has two types of functions: those that can be evaluated quickly in a matrix-free way on the domain (i.e. rank-1 features) and more complex features that must first be decomposed using tensor network (TN) decomposition strategies (tensor features). In particular, we study the effect of adding features which distill pretrained DNN into TNs using a discretize and decompose strategy. To efficiently decompose high-dimensional functions constructed from discretized DNN, we leverage a randomized tensor decomposition strategy. Using randomization, we are able to reduce the storage cost of decomposing high dimensional functions by at least 8 orders of magnitude. Using this approach, we are able to efficiently train models between 5 and 40 dimensions.

AI.tldr: A method to accelerate DNN optimization for high-dimensional functions using contextual features in the first layer, with a two-step alternating optimization between DNN parameters and feature updates, leveraging tensor network decompositions and randomization for efficiency.
AI.motivation: Optimizing deep neural networks for high-dimensional functions is computationally challenging, requiring efficient methods to handle the complexity and storage requirements of such high-dimensional spaces.
AI.method: Introduce contextual features into DNN's first layer. Use alternating optimization: 1) Optimize DNN parameters via gradient descent with fixed features, 2) Update feature layer. Features include fast matrix-free rank-1 features and tensor features requiring TN decomposition. Use randomized tensor decomposition to distill pretrained DNN into tensor networks.
AI.result: Achieved 8+ orders of magnitude reduction in storage cost for decomposing high-dimensional functions. Successfully trained models in 5-40 dimensions efficiently using the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: The method provides an effective way to accelerate DNN optimization for high-dimensional functions through contextual features and randomized tensor network decompositions, enabling efficient training in previously challenging dimensional ranges.

title: DSAgentBench: Can Agents Automate End-to-End Data-Science Workflows in Real Computer Environments?
summary: Real-world data science involves long-horizon workflows that span data wrangling, exploration, modeling, visualization, and validation, and require coordinated use of tools such as notebooks, IDEs, terminals, browsers, and databases within real operating environments. Yet existing benchmarks lack real-computer interaction and do not evaluate whether agents can execute complete end-to-end data-science workflows in realistic computing environments, failing to capture the multi-stage, multi-tool nature of data-science practice. We introduce DSAgentBench, the first benchmark to evaluate whether agents can automate full data-science workflows inside real computer environments. DSAgentBench contains 275 diverse tasks covering the entire data-science life-cycle, reflecting the complexity and tool coordination required in practice. Each task requires grounding decisions in intermediate outputs and coordinated tool use, and includes a deterministic evaluator that verifies analytical correctness, visual outputs, and model performance rather than code-only execution. Our extensive experiments with 15 closed- and open-source models show that even the strongest agent, Claude-4.6-Sonnet, achieves only 56.70% task success, while all open-source agents remain below 1%, frequently failing at tool orchestration, OS grounding, and multi-step reasoning. These results reveal a substantial capability gap between current agentic systems and real data-science workflows, positioning DSAgentBench as a foundation for developing grounded, verifiable, autonomous data-science agents. We release DSAgentBench at https://github.com/vis-nlp/DSAgentBench.

AI.tldr: DSAgentBench is a new benchmark that evaluates whether AI agents can automate complete data science workflows in real computer environments, with results showing current agents struggle significantly with tool orchestration and multi-step reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks lack real computer interaction and fail to evaluate whether agents can execute complete end-to-end data science workflows in realistic computing environments, missing the multi-stage, multi-tool nature of real data science practice.
AI.method: The authors introduce DSAgentBench with 275 diverse tasks covering the entire data science lifecycle, requiring grounding decisions in intermediate outputs and coordinated tool use. Each task includes a deterministic evaluator that verifies analytical correctness, visual outputs, and model performance rather than just code execution.
AI.result: Experiments with 15 closed- and open-source models show that the strongest agent (Claude-4.6-Sonnet) achieves only 56.70% task success, while all open-source agents remain below 1%. Agents frequently fail at tool orchestration, OS grounding, and multi-step reasoning.
AI.conclusion: There's a substantial capability gap between current agentic systems and real data-science workflows. DSAgentBench serves as a foundation for developing grounded, verifiable, autonomous data-science agents and highlights critical areas for improvement in AI agents for complex real-world tasks.

title: Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Tool-Use Agentic Tasks
comment: Published at the COLM 2026 Workshop on Efficient Reasoning
summary: Long-horizon tool-using agents must reason over user goals, domain policies, tool calls, simulator state, and delayed verifiable rewards. Reinforcement learning (RL) is a natural fit for this setting, but multi-turn on-policy rollouts create long contexts, while model-specific attention layers may require custom masks and learned sink normalization. We present SINKFLEX-RL, a modular training system for RL in dual-control tool-use environments. The system combines a Gymnasium-compatible environment wrapper, a VERL-style rollout dataflow, group-relative policy optimization without a separate value model, and a sink-aware FlexAttention path designed to preserve model-specific sink scaling under causal and sliding-window masks. In a preliminary Tau2Bench retail run, validation reward (mean@1) rises from 0.25 early in training to $0.44$ later in the observed training window, while training-score and trajectory-reward proxies also trend upward. In a fixed-configuration memory benchmark, the optimized attention path reduces peak VRAM from 28.06GB to 22.52GB at 4096 tokens, a $19.7\%$ reduction, and runs the measured 8192-token configuration using $25.53$~GB where the eager baseline runs out of memory. These results illustrate the value of integrating environment interfaces, RL dataflow, and attention-kernel design for memory-feasible long-horizon agent training.

AI.tldr: SINKFLEX-RL: A modular training system combining environment wrappers, RL dataflow, and sink-aware attention for memory-efficient long-horizon tool-using agent training.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon tool-using agents face challenges with reasoning over complex elements (user goals, domain policies, tool calls, simulator state, delayed rewards). While RL is suitable, multi-turn on-policy rollouts create long contexts, and model-specific attention layers require custom masks and sink normalization.
AI.method: SINKFLEX-RL combines: 1) Gymnasium-compatible environment wrapper, 2) VERL-style rollout dataflow, 3) group-relative policy optimization without separate value model, and 4) sink-aware FlexAttention path to preserve model-specific sink scaling under causal and sliding-window masks.
AI.result: Validation reward rises from 0.25 to 0.44 in Tau2Bench retail run. In memory benchmark, optimized attention reduces peak VRAM by 19.7% (28.06GB to 22.52GB at 4096 tokens), and runs 8192-token config with 25.53GB where baseline runs out of memory.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the value of integrating environment interfaces, RL dataflow, and attention-kernel design for memory-feasible long-horizon agent training.

title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Diffusion-Based Unrestricted Robotic Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong capabilities in controlling robots across diverse manipulation tasks. However, their adversarial robustness remains largely underexplored, and exploiting this weakness can lead to physical-world harm. Existing attacks on VLA models often rely on pixel-space perturbations or white-box access, resulting in noticeable artifacts and limited deployability in real-world robotic systems. In this work, we propose DURA, a diffusion-based unrestricted robotic attack that generates visually natural adversarial patches for VLA models. DURA supports both white-box and black-box attack settings, where the black-box setting requires only the predicted actions of the victim model. By optimizing along the latent trajectory of a pretrained diffusion model, DURA generates visually natural patches while steering the robot toward attacker-specified target actions. Extensive experiments in both simulation and the real physical world show that DURA consistently outperforms existing methods. Our findings expose a safety risk for physically deployed VLA models and call for stronger defenses.

AI.tldr: DURA is a diffusion-based unrestricted robotic attack that generates visually natural adversarial patches to manipulate Vision-Language-Action models, exposing safety risks in physically deployed robotic systems.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models show strong robotic control capabilities but their adversarial robustness is largely unexplored. Existing attacks have limitations: they often rely on pixel-space perturbations or white-box access, resulting in noticeable artifacts and limited deployability in real-world systems.
AI.method: DURA uses diffusion-based unrestricted adversarial patches. It optimizes along the latent trajectory of a pretrained diffusion model to generate visually natural patches while steering the robot toward attacker-specified target actions. Supports both white-box and black-box settings (black-box only requires predicted actions).
AI.result: Extensive experiments in both simulation and real physical world show DURA consistently outperforms existing methods. The attack effectively exposes safety vulnerabilities in physically deployed VLA models.
AI.conclusion: The findings expose significant safety risks for physically deployed VLA models and call for stronger defense mechanisms to protect robotic systems from such visually natural adversarial attacks.

title: Invertible Logits Transformation for Accuracy-Preserving Post-Hoc Uncertainty Calibration
summary: Post-hoc calibration aligns a classifier's predicted confidences with its empirical accuracy without retraining. An ideal calibrator should correct nonlinear miscalibration, scale gracefully to large label spaces, and preserve the original predictions; existing methods typically violate at least one of these properties---temperature scaling lacks expressivity, more flexible parametric alternatives introduce parameters that grow with the number of classes $C$, and other expressive methods do not preserve the rank ordering of class scores and may alter the predicted class. We propose \textbf{Invertible Logits Transformation (InvLT)}, which applies a learned scalar MLP $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ element-wise to the pre-softmax logits. Sharing $f$ across all logit dimensions makes the parameter count independent of $C$. Monotonicity of $f$---and hence preservation of the argmax prediction---is softly encouraged via a paired inverse network rather than enforced through the numerical integration required by prior monotone calibrators; this avoids their computational overhead while empirically preserving the original classification accuracy in every setting we evaluate. Across standard image classification benchmarks and a range of architectures, InvLT consistently outperforms a broad set of post-hoc baselines on standard calibration metrics.

AI.tldr: InvLT is a post-hoc calibration method that uses a learned monotonic scalar MLP applied element-wise to logits, achieving better calibration than existing methods while preserving class rankings and being scalable to large label spaces.
AI.motivation: Existing post-hoc calibration methods have limitations: temperature scaling lacks expressivity, parametric alternatives have parameters that grow with number of classes, and other methods don't preserve class rankings. An ideal calibrator should correct nonlinear miscalibration, scale to large label spaces, and preserve original predictions.
AI.method: Invertible Logits Transformation (InvLT) applies a learned scalar MLP f:ℝ→ℝ element-wise to pre-softmax logits. Sharing f across all logit dimensions makes parameters independent of class count C. Monotonicity of f (preserving argmax predictions) is encouraged via a paired inverse network rather than enforced through numerical integration.
AI.result: InvLT outperforms a broad set of post-hoc baselines on standard calibration metrics across standard image classification benchmarks and various architectures. It preserves original classification accuracy in every evaluated setting while avoiding computational overhead of prior monotone calibrators.
AI.conclusion: InvLT provides an effective post-hoc calibration solution that combines expressivity, scalability, and prediction preservation, addressing limitations of existing methods while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: Threat-guided Policy-aware Scene Perturbation for Safe Autonomous Driving with Online Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promising performance in autonomous driving, yet ensuring the safety of online RL policies remains challenging due to insufficient exposure to safety-critical driving scenes. The long-tailed nature of real-world traffic situations makes dangerous and rare interactions difficult to encounter through conventional sampling, limiting the ability of RL policies to learn robust safety behaviors. Existing methods improve training diversity by synthesizing challenging scenes or adversarial situations. However, these approaches typically optimize scene generation objectives separately from the evolving policy, without explicitly modeling how generated perturbations relate to the current policy's weaknesses and learning needs. In this paper, we propose Threat-guided Policy-aware Scene Perturbation (TPSP) for safe autonomous driving with online RL. TPSP introduces a policy-aware scene encoder to capture the interaction between policy behaviors and surrounding environments, enabling scene perturbation aligned with the current policy. Based on this representation, TPSP selectively perturbs critical objects rather than applying uniform modifications across the scene. Furthermore, we develop a threat-guided optimization strategy that evaluates perturbed scenes through threat-level differences between policy rollouts on original and perturbed scenes, guiding the generation of safety-critical scenes with higher training value. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that TPSP improves safety learning efficiency, achieving strong safety performance on NAVSIM v2 with approximately 4 million kilometers of simulated driving data. Ablation studies verify that policy-aware targeted perturbations provide more informative safety-critical experiences than random or policy-unaware strategies, enabling safer driving under limited interaction budgets.

AI.tldr: TPSP is a reinforcement learning method that generates targeted safety-critical driving scenes by perturbing specific objects based on current policy weaknesses, improving autonomous driving safety training efficiency.
AI.motivation: Online RL policies for autonomous driving struggle with safety due to insufficient exposure to rare, dangerous traffic scenarios. The long-tailed nature of real-world traffic makes safety-critical interactions difficult to encounter through conventional sampling. Existing scene generation methods don't align perturbations with current policy weaknesses.
AI.method: TPSP uses a policy-aware scene encoder to model interactions between policy behaviors and environments, enabling targeted perturbations of critical objects. It employs threat-guided optimization that evaluates scenes based on threat-level differences between policy rollouts on original vs. perturbed scenes, generating high-value safety-critical scenarios.
AI.result: TPSP improves safety learning efficiency and achieves strong safety performance on NAVSIM v2 with ~4 million kilometers of simulated driving data. Ablation studies show policy-aware targeted perturbations provide more informative safety-critical experiences than random or policy-unaware strategies.
AI.conclusion: By aligning scene perturbations with current policy weaknesses through policy-aware encoding and threat-guided optimization, TPSP enables more efficient safety learning for autonomous driving RL policies, particularly under limited interaction budgets.

title: Fisher8: Stabilizing Neural Heteroscedastic Regression via Output-Layer Fisher Geometry
summary: Training neural networks to jointly predict mean and uncertainty estimates from noisy observations can be unstable, prompting a series of independent stabilization efforts. We argue that these interventions highlight a common underlying issue where gradient steps are poorly aligned with the geometry of the loss landscape. To better align updates with local curvature, we derive Fisher8, an output-layer gradient correction that reorients and rescales updates using Fisher geometry rather than Euclidean geometry. Unlike past stabilizers, Fisher8 introduces no data-dependent hyperparameters beyond learning rate and admits an approximate KL trust radius between successive predictive distributions. We show that prior stabilizers converge on overlapping components of this geometric correction. Across multidimensional regression and representation-learning tasks, Fisher8 obtains superior likelihood--error tradeoffs, predicts calibrated uncertainty estimates, and learns rich uncertainty-aware feature spaces.

AI.tldr: Fisher8 is a new gradient correction method that stabilizes neural network training for joint mean-uncertainty prediction by aligning gradient updates with Fisher geometry rather than Euclidean geometry.
AI.motivation: Training neural networks to jointly predict mean and uncertainty estimates from noisy observations is unstable, and previous stabilization efforts point to a common issue of poorly aligned gradient steps with the loss landscape geometry.
AI.method: Derived Fisher8, an output-layer gradient correction that reorients and rescales updates using Fisher geometry rather than Euclidean geometry. It introduces no data-dependent hyperparameters beyond learning rate and admits an approximate KL trust radius between successive predictive distributions.
AI.result: Fisher8 obtains superior likelihood-error tradeoffs, predicts calibrated uncertainty estimates, and learns rich uncertainty-aware feature spaces across multidimensional regression and representation-learning tasks.
AI.conclusion: Fisher8 provides a principled geometric correction that unifies and improves upon previous stabilization approaches for training neural networks to predict both means and uncertainties, offering better alignment with the loss landscape and improved performance.

title: Reasoning Shortcuts and Value Symmetries: What Symmetry Permits, Architecture Realizes, and Optimization Selects
summary: Reasoning shortcuts are solutions of a neurosymbolic system's rules that produce correct predictions through unintended concepts. A recent framework of Takemura, Inoue, and Nishino analyzes them through an automorphism group of value relabelings and asks, as its central open question, when rules pin concepts down. We first show that the framework's key definition, one shared permutation applied at every position, does not apply as stated to any of the four heterogeneous benchmarks it was evaluated on, and that the most direct embedding, padding domains to a common size, produces confident false pathology: 90.91% of solution pairs reported unexplained on CLE4EVR, where every well-defined member of the hierarchy we introduce reports 0%, and the padded verdict's content rotates with configuration-file ordering. Re-measuring eleven rule families under fifteen pre-specified predictions (thirteen confirmed), unexplained-pair rates span 0% to 99.9999% and track provable structure: six theorems give sufficient conditions for transitivity and its failure, including a Free Slot Lemma certifying Kandinsky's pathology from syntax alone. For circuit-given rules, deciding symmetry-inertness of a coordinate is coNP-complete; nontrivial-automorphism existence is coNP-hard under randomized reductions, lies in $Σ_2^p$, is not $Σ_2^p$-complete unless PH collapses, and on monotone circuits is coNP-complete outright. In the Boolean case transitivity is classified exactly: automorphisms explain everything iff the solution set is an affine coset. Weakly supervised models place all 94 observed shortcuts at the one level the componentwise theory flags and none at the 48 it certifies transitive; twelve typed-ambiguous levels produce none, separating what symmetry permits from what optimization selects, and a dual-head control replicates the geography. All numbers trace to released artifacts.

AI.tldr: The paper critically analyzes the framework for reasoning shortcuts in neurosymbolic systems, revealing flaws in the original definition and introducing a new hierarchy that better explains shortcut phenomena across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address shortcomings in Takemura, Inoue, and Nishino's framework for analyzing reasoning shortcuts, which incorrectly applies to existing benchmarks and produces false pathology. The authors aim to develop a more rigorous understanding of when rules "pin concepts down" and how symmetries explain shortcut behavior.
AI.method: The authors introduce a new hierarchical framework for analyzing reasoning shortcuts, conduct extensive empirical evaluation across 11 rule families and 15 predictions, develop mathematical theorems about transitivity conditions, analyze computational complexity of symmetry detection in circuit-given rules, and perform weakly supervised model experiments to separate what symmetry permits from what optimization selects.
AI.result: Key findings: 1) Original framework doesn't apply to any of four heterogeneous benchmarks; 2) Padding produces false pathology (90.91% unexplained pairs on CLE4EVR vs 0% with new hierarchy); 3) Six theorems provide sufficient conditions for transitivity; 4) Complexity results for symmetry detection (coNP-complete for coordinate symmetry-inertness, coNP-hard for nontrivial-automorphism existence); 5) Boolean transitivity classification (automorphisms explain everything iff solution set is affine coset); 6) Empirical separation shows models place all 94 observed shortcuts at flagged levels, none at certified transitive levels.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a more rigorous foundation for analyzing reasoning shortcuts through symmetry, separating what mathematical structure permits from what optimization selects, with verified results across multiple benchmarks and computational complexity characterizations.

title: Generator-Guided Inverse Sampling for Lévy-Driven Generative Models
summary: This paper studies inverse sampling for Lévy-driven generative models from the perspective of Markov generators. Unlike conventional diffusion models, Lévy-driven dynamics involve infinite jump activities, which makes their reverse process nonlocal and difficult to characterize using score information alone. We address this challenge by analyzing the forward and reversed generators. It is derived that the reversed jump component generally becomes a state-dependent Markov jump process governed by a nonlocal density ratio. This observation motivates a structured reverse sampler that decomposes the dynamics into diffusion, small jump, and large jump components. Based on this characterization, we develop a computationally tractable sampler for a class of isotropic linear Lévy SDEs with symmetric $α$-stable jump components. For the jump component, the neural network is used only to amortize the rate of large jump activities, while jump amplitudes are generated from analytically derived conditional distributions, which improves interpretability and controllability. Efficient implementation techniques are further introduced under this setting to avoid expensive high-dimensional integration and sampling. The sampler is further adapted to approximate observation-guided sampling and applied to OFDM-SISO channel estimation under mixed Gaussian and impulsive noise. Simulations show robust estimation performance with a favorable tradeoff between complexity and performance.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a novel reverse sampler for Lévy-driven generative models by analyzing forward and reversed Markov generators, enabling efficient sampling for α-stable jump processes with improved interpretability.
AI.motivation: Conventional diffusion models cannot effectively handle Lévy-driven dynamics with infinite jump activities, as their reverse processes become nonlocal and challenging to characterize using only score information.
AI.method: The authors analyze forward and reversed Markov generators to derive that reversed jump components become state-dependent Markov jump processes governed by nonlocal density ratios. They develop a structured reverse sampler decomposing dynamics into diffusion, small jump, and large jump components, using neural networks only to amortize large jump rates while deriving conditional distributions analytically for jump amplitudes.
AI.result: The paper develops a computationally tractable sampler for isotropic linear Lévy SDEs with symmetric α-stable jump components, introducing efficient implementation techniques to avoid expensive high-dimensional operations. The method shows robust estimation performance for OFDM-SISO channel estimation under mixed Gaussian and impulsive noise.
AI.conclusion: The generator-based approach provides a principled framework for Lévy-driven generative models, offering improved interpretability and controllability over conventional score-based methods, with practical applications in communication systems under challenging noise conditions.

title: Recovering Wasted Compute in Autoresearch Agents
summary: A slew of recent works develop agents for solving research problems end-to-end, a paradigm increasingly referred to as autoresearch. Such agents have inspired large industry investment, motivated by their potential to automate time-consuming human labor and customize machine learning solutions for specialized applications. In this paper, we study the modeling pipeline at the core of these autoresearch systems and identify common failure modes when they are applied to tabular datasets: (1) they waste compute resolving the same bugs over and over again; (2) they often fail to tune hyperparameters even when they have a large remaining compute budget; (3) the tree-search algorithms that power them do not explore; and (4) they perform data analysis, mimicking the humans whose data they are trained on, but do not use that analysis to make downstream decisions. We explore targeted interventions and find that a global debug consultant that shares discovered runtime constraints across all branches of the search tree, prompt- and control-level enhancements, and refined tree-search algorithms successfully recover wasted compute. Our results show that large gains in autoresearch agent performance are achievable through agentic design alone, holding the underlying language model fixed.

AI.tldr: Autoresearch agents for tabular datasets have common failure modes: repetitive bug fixing, inefficient hyperparameter tuning, poor exploration in tree-search, and unused data analysis. Targeted interventions like global debug consultants and enhanced algorithms can significantly improve performance without changing the underlying language model.
AI.motivation: Autoresearch agents are attracting significant industry investment due to their potential to automate time-consuming human labor and customize ML solutions, but current systems have systematic failure modes when applied to tabular datasets that limit their effectiveness.
AI.method: The authors identify four common failure modes in autoresearch agents for tabular data, then propose targeted interventions including: (1) a global debug consultant that shares runtime constraints across search tree branches, (2) prompt- and control-level enhancements, and (3) refined tree-search algorithms.
AI.result: The interventions successfully recover wasted compute by addressing the identified failure modes. The paper demonstrates that substantial performance improvements in autoresearch agents can be achieved through better agentic design alone, without modifying the underlying language model.
AI.conclusion: Large performance gains in autoresearch agents are achievable through improved agentic design strategies that address systematic failure modes, particularly for tabular datasets. This suggests that current limitations are more about design architecture than fundamental LLM capabilities.

title: Dreamer-SAC: Off-Policy Learning in Latent World Models for Sample-Efficient Autonomous Driving
summary: Sample-efficient reinforcement learning for autonomous driving is often limited by the trade-off between data efficiency and model bias. While world models reduce the reliance on costly environment interactions, policy optimization over learned dynamics remains sensitive to prediction errors. This paper proposes the Dreamer-SAC framework, which integrates a recurrent state-space world model with an off-policy soft actor-critic algorithm trained directly in latent space. The framework uses a combination of real interactions and short-horizon generated trajectories with n-step target estimation and multi-objective supervision. Evaluated in autonomous driving scenarios with objectives encompassing driving efficiency and safety, the proposed framework consistently outperforms representative reinforcement learning baselines, including DreamerV3, SAC, and PPO, while achieving improved performance with substantially fewer real environment interactions. Experiments reveal an inverted-U relationship between rollout horizon and policy performance, where short-horizon latent rollouts achieve the best trade-off between additional training signals and accumulated model bias. Furthermore, n-step target estimation demonstrates more effectiveness over one-step temporal-difference targets in exploiting predicted experience for value learning.

AI.tldr: Dreamer-SAC combines world models with off-policy RL in latent space for sample-efficient autonomous driving, outperforming baselines with fewer real interactions.
AI.motivation: There's a trade-off between data efficiency and model bias in autonomous driving RL. World models reduce costly environment interactions but policy optimization remains sensitive to prediction errors from learned dynamics.
AI.method: The Dreamer-SAC framework integrates recurrent state-space world models with off-policy soft actor-critic algorithm trained directly in latent space. Uses real interactions and short-horizon generated trajectories with n-step target estimation and multi-objective supervision.
AI.result: Outperforms representative RL baselines (DreamerV3, SAC, PPO) in autonomous driving scenarios with driving efficiency and safety objectives. Achieves improved performance with substantially fewer real environment interactions. Found inverted-U relationship between rollout horizon and performance, with short-horizon latent rollouts achieving best trade-off. N-step target estimation more effective than one-step TD targets for value learning.
AI.conclusion: The Dreamer-SAC framework successfully addresses the data efficiency vs. model bias trade-off in autonomous driving RL, demonstrating that carefully designed latent-space training with short-horizon rollouts and n-step estimation can achieve superior sample efficiency while maintaining performance.

title: Conversational versus Dashboard Explainable AI for UAV Intrusion Detection: An Empirical Study of Operator Trust and Reliance
summary: Machine learning-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) have demonstrated superior performance in securing Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks. However, the 'black-box' nature of these models, combined with the high dimensionality of multimodal cyber-physical data, poses significant interpretability challenges. Static visualization dashboards may struggle to present complex relationships among multimodal cyber-physical features in a form that is easy for operators to inspect and interpret. To address this, we propose a Conversational XAI interface powered by Large Language Models (LLM) to facilitate on-demand investigation. In a controlled experiment with participants, we systematically evaluated the impact of this conversational interface versus a traditional XAI Dashboard on operator understanding, trust, and reliance during post-incident auditing tasks. Our results suggest that the conversational interface was perceived as more useful than the dashboard, potentially because it helped participants access and synthesize relevant information more easily. However, this benefit was accompanied by a lower level of appropriate self-reliance, indicating a potential risk of over-reliance. One possible interpretation is that the natural-language responses made the AI advice easier to accept, which may have reduced participants' tendency to verify the underlying evidence when the IDS was incorrect. These findings point to a potential trade-off in human-AI collaboration for UAV intrusion auditing: interaction mechanisms that improve perceived usability may also increase the risk of inappropriate reliance. We conclude by discussing design implications for future XAI systems that balance seamless interaction with cognitive forcing functions to foster appropriate reliance.

AI.tldr: Researchers developed a conversational XAI interface using LLMs for UAV network intrusion detection, finding it improved usability but increased risk of over-reliance compared to traditional dashboards.
AI.motivation: Machine learning-based IDS for UAV networks have 'black-box' nature and high-dimensional multimodal cyber-physical data, making them difficult to interpret. Static visualization dashboards struggle to present complex multimodal feature relationships in an easily interpretable way for operators.
AI.method: Proposed a Conversational XAI interface powered by Large Language Models (LLM) for on-demand investigation. Conducted a controlled experiment comparing this conversational interface against a traditional XAI Dashboard, evaluating operator understanding, trust, and reliance during post-incident auditing tasks.
AI.result: Conversational interface was perceived as more useful than dashboard, helping participants access and synthesize information more easily. However, it led to lower appropriate self-reliance, indicating potential over-reliance risk. Natural-language responses made AI advice easier to accept, reducing participants' tendency to verify evidence when IDS was incorrect.
AI.conclusion: Reveals a trade-off in human-AI collaboration for UAV intrusion auditing: interaction mechanisms improving perceived usability may increase inappropriate reliance risk. Future XAI systems need to balance seamless interaction with cognitive forcing functions to foster appropriate reliance.

title: Share First, Route What Remains: A Unified Framework for Token-Adaptive MoE Computation
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures, and 7 tables; includes supplementary material. Code is available at https://github.com/existence0420/UniF-MoE
summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have recently moved beyond routing a fixed number of complete experts. Shared-expert designs preserve reusable knowledge, fine-grained methods vary computation within experts, and dynamic routers adapt the number of active experts. Yet these decisions are usually made independently, overlooking a basic dependency: extracting reusable computation changes both what remains and how much expert capacity the remainder needs. We study this dependency by decomposing sparsely upcycled feed-forward experts into key-value channels. Co-activated experts align at a subset of value positions; removing these positions changes expert preference; and greater shared coverage is associated with lower residual expert demand. These observations lead to one principle: share first, then route what remains. We instantiate it in UniF-MoE, a unified framework for token-adaptive MoE computation. Each expert is partitioned into aligned blocks. A shared-demand score sets the shared block count and pathway weight, key prototypes select the shared content, and the complementary demand determines the residual expert count through cumulative routing mass. A Gram regularizer separates and normalizes router embeddings, promoting diverse routing directions, sparse expert overlap, and a simple routing geometry. Experiments on DomainBed and GLUE show that this unified design improves predictive performance over representative static and dynamic MoEs while reducing activated computation, inference latency, and memory. Code is available at https://github.com/existence0420/UniF-MoE.

AI.tldr: UniF-MoE introduces a unified framework that shares computation first via aligned expert blocks, then routes residual demands, improving efficiency and performance over existing MoE approaches.
AI.motivation: Current MoE designs make independent decisions about shared experts, fine-grained computation, and dynamic routing, overlooking the fundamental dependency that extracting reusable computation changes both what remains and how much expert capacity is needed for the remainder.
AI.method: Decompose sparsely upcycled feed-forward experts into key-value channels; partition experts into aligned blocks; use shared-demand score to set shared block count and pathway weight; employ key prototypes to select shared content; use complementary demand to determine residual expert count via cumulative routing mass; apply Gram regularizer to separate and normalize router embeddings.
AI.result: Experiments on DomainBed and GLUE benchmarks show that UniF-MoE improves predictive performance over representative static and dynamic MoEs while reducing activated computation, inference latency, and memory usage.
AI.conclusion: The "share first, then route what remains" principle effectively addresses the overlooked dependency in MoE designs, leading to a unified framework that achieves better performance with reduced computational costs.

title: Continuous Interaction Diffusion: A Diffusion-Native Runtime for Asynchronous Tool-Augmented Reasoning
summary:
Large language models increasingly rely on external tools to access up-to-date information, perform computation, and interact with the outside world. For autoregressive models, tool use naturally fits the generation process: the model emits a tool call, waits for the result, and then continues generating. Diffusion language models (dLLMs), however, reason by repeatedly refining many parts of their output in parallel, making this stop-and-resume interaction pattern unnecessarily restrictive. It can force tool decisions before the model's reasoning has stabilized, delay useful observations until a discrete call finishes, and introduce redundant refinement and tool execution, potentially hurting both task accuracy and inference efficiency.
  We introduce Continuous Interaction Diffusion (CID), a diffusion-native model--runtime architecture that integrates tool interaction into iterative denoising. CID separates a model-read-only fact channel, a thought channel represented by a Typed Cognitive Tensor, and a display channel. Information needs can emerge before a textual or JSON call is fully serialized, allowing perceptual bindings to launch external reads while denoising continues. Returned results are projected into the evolving thought state and can revise earlier cognition and display regions. Persistent bindings reuse static results without repeated external execution and refresh changing sources when needed. CID is designed to expose evidence earlier, overlap tool latency with model computation, reduce duplicate external work, and preserve useful computation after new evidence arrives. We formalize the architecture, runtime, and training objectives, and define an evaluation protocol for task quality and end-to-end efficiency. This first paper focuses on read-only tools and makes no empirical performance claims.

AI.tldr: CID is a new architecture that integrates tool interaction directly into diffusion language models' iterative denoising process, enabling continuous interaction with external tools rather than the traditional stop-and-resume pattern used by autoregressive models.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses a fundamental limitation in diffusion language models' tool usage: their parallel refinement approach conflicts with the sequential stop-and-resume interaction pattern of autoregressive models, forcing early tool decisions, delaying observations, and causing redundant refinement/tool execution that hurts both accuracy and efficiency.
AI.method: CID introduces a diffusion-native model-runtime architecture with three channels: a read-only fact channel, a thought channel using Typed Cognitive Tensors, and a display channel. It allows information needs to emerge before full tool call serialization, enabling perceptual bindings to launch external reads during denoising. Results are projected into evolving thought states and can revise earlier cognition. Persistent bindings reuse static results and refresh changing sources as needed.
AI.result: The paper formalizes the CID architecture, runtime, and training objectives, and defines an evaluation protocol for task quality and end-to-end efficiency. This initial work focuses on read-only tools and makes no empirical performance claims, presenting it as foundational theoretical work.
AI.conclusion: CID represents a promising new approach to tool integration for diffusion language models that could expose evidence earlier, overlap tool latency with computation, reduce duplicate external work, and preserve useful computation after new evidence arrives - addressing fundamental inefficiencies in current approaches.

title: ELVAE: Evidential Learning-Based Variational Autoencoder for Uncertainty-Aware Generation
summary: Variational autoencoders generate samples from probabilistic latent representations but do not distinguish uncertainty about the latent location from variability around it. We formulate ELVAE, an evidential learning-based VAE in which each latent coordinate is governed by an input-dependent normal-inverse-gamma posterior. This hierarchy yields an explicit latent-location uncertainty that can be used during generation, not merely reported after inference: low-uncertainty anchors support more reliable synthetic samples, while high-uncertainty anchors can be deliberately exploited for stress testing. The objective is an exact evidence lower bound, and we show that direct regularization of the full hierarchy is required, since the marginalized latent law alone cannot identify the uncertainty decomposition. In an MNIST generation pilot with a frozen external classifier, this uncertainty clearly stratified the semantic reliability of generated digits. A zero-displacement control revealed that most of the effect reflects how reliably an anchor can be re-generated, while a smaller but distinct component is attributable to uncertainty-scaled perturbation itself. The effect holds only under within-class uncertainty ranking, and its magnitude varies across seeds. These findings support the learned latent-location uncertainty as a practical control variable for uncertainty-aware generation, separating anchor reliability from perturbation-induced failure.

AI.tldr: ELVAE introduces an evidential learning-based VAE that explicitly models latent-location uncertainty, enabling uncertainty-aware generation where low-uncertainty anchors produce reliable samples and high-uncertainty ones can be used for stress testing.
AI.motivation: Standard VAEs don't distinguish between uncertainty about latent location and variability around it. This limits their ability to provide explicit control over uncertainty during generation, which could be useful for reliability assessment and stress testing.
AI.method: ELVAE uses a normal-inverse-gamma posterior for each latent coordinate, creating an input-dependent hierarchical structure. The approach requires direct regularization of the full hierarchy and uses an exact evidence lower bound. Evaluation includes MNIST generation with a frozen classifier, zero-displacement control experiments, and within-class uncertainty ranking.
AI.result: The learned latent-location uncertainty clearly stratified semantic reliability of generated MNIST digits. Most effect comes from anchor regeneration reliability, with a smaller distinct component from uncertainty-scaled perturbation. The effect holds only under within-class uncertainty ranking and varies across seeds.
AI.conclusion: ELVAE's explicit latent-location uncertainty serves as a practical control variable for uncertainty-aware generation, effectively separating anchor reliability from perturbation-induced failure, enabling more reliable synthetic samples and targeted stress testing.
