AI.conclusion: The proposed approach provides an efficient, scalable solution for inverse reinforcement learning by combining Fisher-based hypergradient computation with spectral sketching techniques, making bilevel optimization more practical for IRL applications.

title: SkillZip: Evaluation-Free Skill Compression for Self-Evolving Agents by Discovering Reusable Structure
summary: Self-evolving agents accumulate reusable skills by appending successful procedures and failure fixes. Over time, the same requirement is often restated in several branches, examples, and warnings, while common action sequences are copied rather than reused. The resulting skill becomes expensive to inject and difficult to maintain. Generic prompt compression is ill-suited to this setting because a skill is not a flat passage: its name and description define when it applies, its workflow controls execution, its tool and output contracts constrain validity, and rare exceptions may remain essential even when no sampled task activates them. Evaluation-guided compression can test these behaviors, but it introduces rollouts, cost, and dependence on the compression-time evaluation set. We present SkillZip, an evaluation-free method that compresses a skill by finding its shortest faithful structural explanation. The intuition is explain once, reference many: state a repeated rule once at the scope where it applies, factor a repeated action sequence into a shared procedure, and keep only the differences as explicit exceptions. We formalize this intuition as a typed minimum description-length objective over a skill contract and a residual, subject to a hard coverage constraint for every extracted trigger, workflow edge, tool requirement, obligation, and output field. The formulation provides simple sharing thresholds, preserves unique rare rules by construction, and supports efficient local updates. SkillZip has a one-shot mode with one structured extraction call and deterministic optimization, and a continual Zip-on-Write mode that integrates each self-evolution patch without replaying tasks or reparsing the full history. Through comprehensive experimental evaluations, we demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of SkillZip in compression performance, generalizability, and cost overhead.

AI.tldr: SkillZip is an evaluation-free method that compresses self-evolving AI agent skills by finding the shortest faithful structural explanation, enabling efficient reuse and maintenance while preserving essential behaviors.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving agents accumulate skills over time, leading to redundancy where the same requirements are restated multiple times and common action sequences are copied rather than reused. This makes skills expensive to inject and difficult to maintain. Existing prompt compression methods are unsuitable because skills have complex structure (names, descriptions, workflows, contracts, exceptions), and evaluation-guided compression introduces high costs and dependency on evaluation sets.
AI.method: SkillZip compresses skills by finding their shortest faithful structural explanation based on the principle "explain once, reference many." It formalizes this as a typed minimum description-length objective over a skill contract and residual, with hard coverage constraints for every extracted trigger, workflow edge, tool requirement, obligation, and output field. The method has two modes: one-shot (single structured extraction call with deterministic optimization) and continual Zip-on-Write (integrates each self-evolution patch without replaying tasks or reparsing full history).
AI.result: Through comprehensive experimental evaluations, SkillZip demonstrates effectiveness and superiority in compression performance, generalizability, and cost overhead compared to other methods.
AI.conclusion: SkillZip provides an efficient, evaluation-free approach to compressing self-evolving agent skills that preserves essential behaviors while eliminating redundancy, enabling better skill reuse and maintainability without the costs and dependencies of evaluation-guided compression.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Deep Learning for Genomics Applications: Insights from an Empirical Study
comment: 21 main pages, 42 total pages, 12 main figures, 13 supplementary figures
summary: Deep learning models have emerged as the standard computational tool for a wide range of applications in genomics. Yet, uncertainty quantification (UQ) -- and more specifically, the reliability of different uncertainty estimates in this domain -- has received little systematic attention. This work presents an empirical analysis of UQ in deep learning models, focusing on genomics applications. In a series of experiments, we contrast Deep Ensembles, Bayesian Neural Networks, and Monte Carlo-dropout methods. We assess their ability to quantify uncertainty in different scenarios, accounting for common dataset characteristics in two genomic application areas and modalities: sequence-to-activity models, and single-cell expression analysis. Our systematic comparison framework provides guidelines for the applicability and reliability of UQ methods in genomics, highlighting their strengths and limitations in different scenarios. We show that Bayesian Neural Networks are better at capturing uncertainty caused by strong class imbalance and out-of-distribution data in genomics, despite their computational disadvantages. Moreover, we show how uncertainty scores can be used to select high-quality predictions in protein-RNA interactions.

AI.tldr: Systematic empirical analysis shows Bayesian Neural Networks outperform Deep Ensembles and Monte Carlo-dropout for uncertainty quantification in genomics, especially for class imbalance and out-of-distribution data, with practical applications in protein-RNA interaction quality selection.
AI.motivation: Despite deep learning becoming standard in genomics, uncertainty quantification (UQ) and the reliability of different uncertainty estimates in this domain have received little systematic attention, creating a need for empirical evaluation of UQ methods specific to genomics applications.
AI.method: The authors conducted an empirical analysis comparing three UQ methods: Deep Ensembles, Bayesian Neural Networks, and Monte Carlo-dropout. They assessed these methods on two genomic application areas and modalities: sequence-to-activity models and single-cell expression analysis, accounting for common dataset characteristics in genomics.
AI.result: Bayesian Neural Networks performed better at capturing uncertainty caused by strong class imbalance and out-of-distribution data in genomics, despite their computational disadvantages. The study also demonstrated how uncertainty scores can be used to select high-quality predictions in protein-RNA interactions.
AI.conclusion: The systematic comparison framework provides guidelines for the applicability and reliability of UQ methods in genomics, highlighting their strengths and limitations in different scenarios. Bayesian Neural Networks are particularly effective for certain genomics challenges despite computational costs.

title: RTSKG: Building a Rail Transit Station Knowledge Graph Dataset
summary: Rail transit systems play a vital role in urban mobility and economic development. As key components of such systems, rail transit stations function as critical transport hubs that enhance urban accessibility and stimulate development in surrounding areas. City-level rail transit station related tasks (e.g., ridership prediction) require large-scale urban data, but current studies often neglect complex interactions among various urban entities in terms of data organization. In this paper, to address the above issue, we build a Rail Transit Station Knowledge Graph (RTSKG) dataset which explicitly models the spatial and semantic interactions among different kinds of urban entities, to benefit city-level rail transit station related tasks. RTSKG integrates heterogeneous urban entities, such as rail transit stations, road segments, and points of interest, with a specially designed unified schema, and is accessible as Linked Data at https://w3id.org/rtskg/. Evaluations on station-area store recommendation and knowledge-enhanced ridership prediction demonstrate the effectiveness of RTSKG, highlighting its potential to support city-level rail transit station analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RTSKG, a Rail Transit Station Knowledge Graph dataset that models spatial-semantic interactions between urban entities to enhance city-level rail transit station analysis tasks like ridership prediction.
AI.motivation: Current studies on city-level rail transit station tasks often neglect complex interactions among various urban entities in terms of data organization, despite the need for large-scale urban data.
AI.method: The authors build a Rail Transit Station Knowledge Graph (RTSKG) dataset that explicitly models spatial and semantic interactions among different urban entities (stations, road segments, POIs) using a specially designed unified schema, and make it available as Linked Data.
AI.result: RTSKG demonstrates effectiveness through evaluations on station-area store recommendation and knowledge-enhanced ridership prediction, showing its potential to support city-level rail transit station analysis.
AI.conclusion: The proposed RTSKG dataset successfully addresses data organization limitations by modeling complex urban entity interactions, proving valuable for urban planning and transportation analysis tasks related to rail transit stations.

title: Batch Size or Negatives? A Selection Rule for Memory-Constrained Recommender Training
summary:
Large-scale neural recommender systems are typically trained with a softmax cross-entropy objective over the full item vocabulary. For a typical large number of possible items $K$, the final classification layer dominates memory, requiring $O(nK)$ logits and gradients to materialize for a batch of $n$ examples. Sampled softmax reduces this cost by restricting the objective to only $k \ll K$ candidate negative items, resulting in an $O(nk)$ memory. However, for a fixed budget $B = n k$, it remains unclear whether one should prioritize larger batches or the inclusion of more negative items.
  We address this question by analyzing sampled-softmax training under a fixed memory constraint. Under standard smoothness and variance assumptions, our theoretical evidence suggests that the fastest convergence arises from an $ n \sim B, k \sim 1$ allocation. So, an actionable rule is to include as many objects as possible given computational constraints.
  Our theory is supported by controlled synthetic and synthetic and four real sequential recommendation benchmarks, including MovieLens-20M. The suggested configuration achieve faster convergence and better final recommendation quality than imbalanced alternatives within the same memory constraint. These findings provide a theoretical and empirical foundation for configuring memory during the training of recommender systems. Code, reproducibility materials, and all scripts for generating figures are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LimitedMemoryRule-BBFB

AI.tldr: Under fixed memory constraints for training neural recommenders, optimal convergence comes from maximizing batch size (n) while minimizing negative samples (k), following an n ∼ B, k ∼ 1 allocation rule.
AI.motivation: Large-scale neural recommender systems face memory bottlenecks from the softmax final layer, which requires O(nK) memory. While sampled softmax reduces this to O(nk), there's no clear guidance on how to allocate fixed memory budget B = nk between batch size (n) and negative samples (k) for optimal training.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of sampled-softmax training under fixed memory constraints, supported by experiments on synthetic data and four real sequential recommendation benchmarks (including MovieLens-20M). The approach compares different n,k allocations within the same memory budget B = nk.
AI.result: Under standard smoothness and variance assumptions, the analysis shows fastest convergence arises from n ∼ B, k ∼ 1 allocation. This configuration achieves faster convergence and better final recommendation quality than imbalanced alternatives within the same memory constraint.
AI.conclusion: For neural recommender training under memory constraints, practitioners should prioritize maximizing batch size while keeping negative samples minimal (≈1). This provides a theoretical and empirical foundation for memory configuration in recommender system training, with code and reproducibility materials available.

title: Why Does CLAUDE.md Keep Growing? Catastrophic Remembering in Agentic Coding
summary: Agentic coding READMEs like CLAUDE.md grow without bound in real repositories, stopping only when the repository retires or someone rewrites the file wholesale. We trace this to imperfect recall: appending an instruction is always cheap, but once an instruction's rationale is gone, deleting it without risking a correctness regression costs O(2^|D|) in a prompt of |D| instructions. We name the resulting divergence catastrophic remembering, the inverse of catastrophic forgetting around which continual learning is organized. First, we characterize this phenomenon across 247,694 instruction lifetimes in 1,867 repositories: agentic prompts grow without bound, more than tripling over their lifetime (+226%), gaining +4.9 net instructions every commit; further, the older an instruction gets, the less likely it is to be deleted (log-hazard -0.032/commit). Then, we show that prompt comments can halt the growth: inverting IFEval yields verifiable worlds whose optimal prompts are known, and there comments encoding latent reasoning remove 99.3% of excess instructions (+211.3% to +1.4%). Finally, applying the same inversion to WildIFEval, we show that prompt comments can improve real-world agentic instruction-following by up to 23.1%. If English is the new code, why don't we have comments yet?

AI.tldr: Agentic coding prompts (like CLAUDE.md files) grow uncontrollably over time due to imperfect recall - it's cheap to add instructions but expensive to delete them safely. The paper shows this "catastrophic remembering" phenomenon and demonstrates that prompt comments can halt growth and improve agent performance.
AI.motivation: Agentic coding READMEs (like CLAUDE.md) grow without bound in real repositories, only stopping when repositories retire or files get rewritten. This is problematic because as prompts grow longer, they become less efficient and potentially contradictory. The paper aims to understand and solve this uncontrolled growth of agent instructions.
AI.method:
1. Empirical analysis of 247,694 instruction lifetimes across 1,867 repositories to characterize the growth phenomenon.
2. Use of IFEval inversion to create verifiable worlds with known optimal prompts, then test whether prompt comments can reduce excess instructions.
3. Application of the same approach to WildIFEval to test real-world agentic instruction-following improvement.
AI.result:
1. Agentic prompts more than triple in size over their lifetime (+226%), gaining +4.9 net instructions per commit.
2. Older instructions become exponentially harder to delete (log-hazard decreases by -0.032 per commit).
3. Prompt comments remove 99.3% of excess instructions (reducing growth from +211.3% to +1.4%).
4. In WildIFEval, prompt comments improve real-world agentic instruction-following by up to 23.1%.
AI.conclusion: The paper identifies "catastrophic remembering" as the inverse of catastrophic forgetting, showing that prompt growth is a fundamental problem in agentic coding. The solution is prompt comments - just as code comments help human developers understand rationale, prompt comments enable agents to safely delete outdated instructions. This addresses the paper's final question: "If English is the new code, why don't we have comments yet?"

title: Cross-View Feature Matching: Survey, Benchmarking, and Foundation-Model Perspectives
comment: This manuscript goes beyond a conventional survey. It proposes a new taxonomy for cross-view feature matching, provides extensive benchmarking under unified datasets and protocols, and offers original analysis from the perspective of vision foundation models. These contributions provide substantive methodological synthesis, empirical findings, and new research insights
summary: Cross-view feature matching aims to establish reliable correspondences across images with large viewpoint variations. Over the past decade, the field has evolved from task-specific models toward increasingly unified and generalizable correspondence models, with recent progress further driven by the emergence of vision foundation models (VFMs). Despite these advances, existing studies remain highly diverse in their problem formulations, model architectures, training paradigms, and evaluation protocols, making it difficult to obtain a unified understanding of the field. In this survey, we present a unified review of cross-view feature matching. We first introduce a structured taxonomy covering feature extraction, single-type feature matcher, multi-type feature matcher, VFMs based methods, training strategy and robust estimation, providing a coherent framework for analysis and comparison. We further examine recent advances, distilling key design principles and highlighting the shift toward unified and generalizable correspondence models. We also provide a unified experimental benchmarking of representative state-of-the-art methods under consistent protocols, enabling fair and comprehensive performance comparisons. In addition, we discuss open challenges and future directions, including efficiency, robustness under extreme conditions, and cross-domain generalization. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive and structured reference for understanding the evolution, current landscape, and future development of cross-view feature matching in the era of vision foundation models.

AI.tldr: This is a survey paper providing a unified review and taxonomy of cross-view feature matching methods, analyzing the evolution from task-specific models to unified generalizable correspondence models driven by vision foundation models.
AI.motivation: Despite advances in cross-view feature matching, existing studies remain highly diverse in problem formulations, model architectures, training paradigms, and evaluation protocols, making it difficult to obtain a unified understanding of the field. The emergence of vision foundation models has further driven recent progress, but there's a need for structured analysis and fair benchmarking.
AI.method: The authors create a structured taxonomy covering feature extraction, single-type feature matchers, multi-type feature matchers, VFM-based methods, training strategies, and robust estimation. They provide unified experimental benchmarking of representative state-of-the-art methods under consistent protocols and distill key design principles.
AI.result: The survey presents a comprehensive framework for analyzing cross-view feature matching, highlights the shift toward unified and generalizable correspondence models, and enables fair performance comparisons through consistent benchmarking protocols.
AI.conclusion: This survey provides a structured reference for understanding the evolution and current landscape of cross-view feature matching, discussing open challenges including efficiency, robustness under extreme conditions, and cross-domain generalization in the era of vision foundation models.

title: sLTN: Structural Logic Tensor Networks
summary: Logic Tensor Networks (LTN) provide a neurosymbolic framework in which first-order logic is interpreted through tensor operations, enabling logical constraints to be integrated with differentiable learning. However, the original formulation of LTN is primarily suited to data represented as flat collections of individuals, and does not explicitly capture structural organization such as temporal order, sequential position, or graph connectivity. We introduce sLTN, an extension of LTN that makes structural dimensions first-class elements of the language. Structural dimensions represent named tensor axes associated with domain-specific organization, such as time steps, sequence positions, or graph nodes. They can be quantified explicitly, related through structural relations, and used to express temporal, sequential, and relational constraints directly at the logical level. We formalize the syntax and fuzzy tensor semantics of sLTN and show that, in the absence of structural dimensions, the framework recovers the original LTN semantics as a special case. We further describe a PyTorch implementation based on a declarative signature, formula parsing, and tensorial interpretation. The framework is illustrated on representative temporal and sequential reasoning examples. This paper serves as a companion to the sltn library, available at https://github.com/logictensornetworks/sltn.

AI.tldr: sLTN extends Logic Tensor Networks by adding structural dimensions as first-class elements to capture temporal, sequential, and graph structure, with a PyTorch implementation available.
AI.motivation: The original LTN framework is limited to flat data representations and doesn't explicitly handle structural organization like temporal order, sequential position, or graph connectivity, which are essential for many real-world reasoning tasks.
AI.method: Introduces sLTN extension with structural dimensions as named tensor axes representing domain-specific organization (time steps, sequence positions, graph nodes). These dimensions can be quantified, related through structural relations, and used to express constraints directly in logic. Formalizes syntax and fuzzy tensor semantics, and implements in PyTorch with declarative signatures, formula parsing, and tensorial interpretation.
AI.result: Creates a framework that recovers original LTN semantics as a special case when structural dimensions are absent. Demonstrates the framework on temporal and sequential reasoning examples. Provides an open-source implementation (sltn library).
AI.conclusion: sLTN successfully extends neurosymbolic reasoning to structured domains by making structural dimensions first-class citizens, enabling direct expression of temporal, sequential, and relational constraints while maintaining backward compatibility with LTN.

title: Two-stage Odd Residual Flows for Mean-Preserving Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
summary: Probabilistic forecasting plays an essential role in risk-sensitive decision-making, particularly in long-horizon settings. However, existing approaches often face a fundamental trade-off between distributional flexibility and accurate mean prediction. Traditional parametric methods, such as Mean Variance Estimation (MVE), can suffer from degraded point accuracy when trained under joint Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) objectives, while modern-flexible generative models, including Normalizing Flows and Diffusion Models, typically rely on costly Monte Carlo sampling and may yield suboptimal mean estimates. To address this limitation, we propose Two-stage Odd Residual Flows (TORF), a framework that decouples mean forecasting from uncertainty estimation. In the first stage, a pre-trained deterministic model is used to produce an accurate mean prediction. In the second stage, a Restricted Normalizing Flow, with strictly odd functions learns flexible residual distributions around the point forecast, guaranteeing mean preservation from the first stage without sampling. Experiments show that TORF achieves state-of-the-art deterministic accuracy (NMAE) while providing strong density estimation performance (CRPS) on short and long-horizon forecasting.

AI.tldr: TORF is a two-stage probabilistic forecasting framework that separates mean prediction from uncertainty estimation to overcome the trade-off between distributional flexibility and mean accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing probabilistic forecasting methods face a fundamental trade-off: traditional parametric methods (like MVE) suffer degraded point accuracy when trained with joint NLL objectives, while flexible generative models (Normalizing Flows/Diffusion) require costly Monte Carlo sampling and yield suboptimal mean estimates.
AI.method: Two-stage Odd Residual Flows (TORF) decouples mean forecasting from uncertainty estimation. Stage 1 uses a pre-trained deterministic model for accurate mean prediction. Stage 2 uses a Restricted Normalizing Flow with strictly odd functions to learn flexible residual distributions around the point forecast, guaranteeing mean preservation without sampling.
AI.result: TORF achieves state-of-the-art deterministic accuracy (NMAE) while providing strong density estimation performance (CRPS) on both short and long-horizon forecasting tasks.
AI.conclusion: TORF successfully addresses the flexibility-accuracy trade-off in probabilistic forecasting by separating mean prediction and uncertainty estimation, achieving superior performance in both point accuracy and distributional modeling without requiring costly sampling.

title: Long-Horizon AI Research for Grothendieck Constant: A Case Study in Human-AI Mathematical Collaboration

AI.tldr: AI agents were successfully used to improve bounds on the Grothendieck constant, demonstrating effective AI-human collaboration in mathematics research.
AI.motivation: AI agents are increasingly used in mathematics research, but it's often unclear how to use them effectively. The paper aims to provide practical insights into using AI for mathematical discovery by presenting a detailed case study.
AI.method: The researchers used an AI research system to explore and prove bounds on the Grothendieck constant. They conducted an extensive case study documenting their experience with AI-human collaboration in mathematics.
AI.result: The AI system helped tighten the best known bounds for the Grothendieck constant to: 6π/11 ≤ K_G ≤ π/[2log(1+√2)] - 10⁻⁴. The improvements were achieved with AI-derived insights that domain experts deemed novel.
AI.conclusion: AI can be effectively used in mathematics research to arrive at novel insights, but requires careful design of research conditions and understanding of both AI strengths and limitations. The case study provides valuable lessons for AI-human collaboration in mathematical discovery.

title: A Recommendation System Approach for Interference-Robust Sensor Subset Selection
summary: This paper develops a method for sensor-subset selection for tracking. Prior work showed that low-cost acoustic Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) measurements can be used to recommend subsets of sensor nodes whose expensive sensing modalities, such as cameras, can achieve high tracking accuracy. While efficient, RSSI-based approaches are challenged by acoustic interference. We propose a recommendation-system-inspired framework that instead leverages frequency-band acoustic features and a Two-Tower Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architecture to efficiently score candidate sensor subsets. Experimental results on outdoor vehicle-tracking deployments show that the proposed method can improve accuracy by around 20\% over the RSSI baseline while maintaining the low computational overhead required for real-time selective sensing.

AI.tldr: A recommendation-system-inspired method for selecting optimal sensor subsets using acoustic frequency features and a Two-Tower MLP architecture improves vehicle tracking accuracy by 20% over RSSI baselines while maintaining real-time computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: Previous RSSI-based sensor selection methods for tracking are efficient but vulnerable to acoustic interference, limiting their reliability in real-world deployments where accurate sensor subset selection is crucial for balancing tracking accuracy with computational/resource constraints.
AI.method: Proposes a recommendation-system-inspired framework that uses frequency-band acoustic features instead of RSSI. Uses a Two-Tower Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architecture to efficiently score candidate sensor subsets, enabling real-time selection of optimal sensor combinations for tracking.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation on outdoor vehicle-tracking deployments shows the method improves accuracy by approximately 20% over RSSI baseline approaches while maintaining low computational overhead suitable for real-time selective sensing applications.
AI.conclusion: The proposed recommendation-system framework with frequency-band features and Two-Tower MLP architecture effectively addresses acoustic interference limitations of RSSI methods, providing significantly improved tracking accuracy while preserving the computational efficiency needed for real-world sensor network deployments.

title: The Gaussian-Multinoulli Restricted Boltzmann Machine: A Potts Model Extension of the GRBM
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures (1 figure has 2 subfigures), conference
summary: Many real-world tasks, from associative memory to symbolic reasoning, benefit from discrete, structured representations that standard continuous latent models can struggle to express. We introduce the Gaussian-Multinoulli Restricted Boltzmann Machine (GM-RBM), a generative energy-based model that extends the Gaussian-Bernoulli RBM (GB-RBM) by replacing binary hidden units with q-state categorical (Potts) units, yielding a richer latent state space for multivalued concepts. We provide a self-contained derivation of the energy, conditional distributions, and learning rules, and detail practical training choices (contrastive divergence with temperature annealing and intra-slot diversity constraints) that avoid state collapse. To separate architectural effects from sheer latent capacity, we evaluate under both capacity-matched and parameter-matched setups, comparing GM-RBM with GB-RBM configured to have the same number of possible latent assignments. On analogical recall and structured memory benchmarks, GM-RBM achieves competitive, and in several regimes improved, recall at equal capacity with comparable training cost, despite using only Gibbs updates. The discrete q-ary formulation is also amenable to efficient implementation. These results clarify when categorical hidden units provide a simple, scalable alternative to binary latents for discrete inference within tractable RBMs.

AI.tldr: GM-RBM extends Gaussian-Bernoulli RBM with categorical hidden units for richer discrete representations, showing improved performance on structured tasks at equal capacity with comparable training cost.
AI.motivation: Many real-world tasks require discrete, structured representations that standard continuous latent models struggle to express effectively. The authors aim to create a richer latent state space for multivalued concepts.
AI.method: Introduces Gaussian-Multinoulli RBM (GM-RBM) by replacing binary hidden units with q-state categorical (Potts) units. Provides complete derivation of energy functions, conditional distributions, and learning rules. Uses practical training methods: contrastive divergence with temperature annealing and intra-slot diversity constraints to prevent state collapse.
AI.result: GM-RBM achieves competitive and often improved recall performance on analogical recall and structured memory benchmarks. It performs well under both capacity-matched and parameter-matched setups compared to GB-RBM with same latent capacity. Achieves these results with only Gibbs updates and has comparable training cost.
AI.conclusion: Categorical hidden units provide a simple, scalable alternative to binary latents for discrete inference within tractable RBMs, particularly when richer discrete representations are needed for structured tasks.

title: DACRI: Decision-Aware Causal Intervention Ranking for Critical Supply Chains
comment: Accepted for presentation at the International Conference on Electrical, Computer, Communications and Mechatronics Engineering (ICECCME 2026), 15--17 October 2026, Bali, Indonesia. 5 tables; no figures. Benchmark and code: https://github.com/dyshang/dacri-criticalscm-bench
summary: Detecting or attributing a supply-chain disruption is not the same as selecting the intervention that maximizes recoverable net value. We present CriticalSCM-Bench v1, a controlled synthetic benchmark with causal ground truth, paired factual/counterfactual rollouts, and an explicit net-value objective. Relative to a full-information train-selected static benchmark, LambdaMART improves median normalized net value by 5.7--16.2\%, with paired statistical support on the semiconductor and critical-material archetypes but not on digital infrastructure. On digital infrastructure, a domain-informed constant-buffer policy remains stronger, showing that greater model complexity is not uniformly justified. Across partial and delayed settings, LambdaMART retains 33--75\% of full-clamp value. Stress tests further show that intervention fidelity, timing, cost, and held-out disruptions can alter policy ordering. Critical materials show the weakest out-of-distribution retention. Separately, a guarded explanation study over 540 generations preserves every fixed intervention decision after deterministic validation and template fallback, although exact wording remains unstable. Within this controlled setting, the results identify regimes in which adaptive ranking adds value and those in which simpler structural policies remain preferable.

AI.tldr: CriticalSCM-Bench v1 benchmark shows LambdaMART improves median normalized net value by 5.7-16.2% for semiconductor and critical materials, but domain-informed constant-buffer policies remain stronger for digital infrastructure.
AI.motivation: Current supply chain disruption approaches focus on detection or attribution rather than selecting interventions that maximize recoverable net value. There's a need for controlled benchmarks with causal ground truth to evaluate intervention effectiveness.
AI.method: Created CriticalSCM-Bench v1, a controlled synthetic benchmark with causal ground truth, paired factual/counterfactual rollouts, and explicit net-value objective. Used LambdaMART ranking model compared against full-information train-selected static benchmarks across semiconductor, critical-material, and digital infrastructure archetypes.
AI.result: LambdaMART improved median normalized net value by 5.7-16.2% for semiconductor and critical materials with statistical significance, but not for digital infrastructure where constant-buffer policies remained stronger. In partial/delayed settings, LambdaMART retained 33-75% of full-clamp value. Critical materials showed weakest out-of-distribution retention.
AI.conclusion: Results identify specific regimes where adaptive ranking adds value and where simpler structural policies remain preferable. Greater model complexity isn't uniformly justified, and intervention characteristics (fidelity, timing, cost, held-out disruptions) can alter policy effectiveness ordering.

title: Hierarchical Empirical-Bayes Naive Bayes: Minimax Smoothing and Calibration with AODE Extension
comment: This manuscript has been submitted to the Knowledge-Based Systems
summary: The Naive Bayes (NB) classifier remains a standard choice for categorical data, yet its widely used smoothing rules, such as Laplace, Lidstone, Krichevsky-Trofimov, and the $m$-estimate, all prescribe a fixed smoothing strength that ignores feature cardinality, sample size, and class imbalance, inducing a non-vanishing bias on modern high-cardinality tabular data. We propose hierarchical empirical-Bayes Naive Bayes (HEB-NB), in which each class-feature conditional probability is smoothed by a Dirichlet prior whose concentration is learned data-adaptively via Type-II maximum likelihood, enabling principled information sharing across classes while retaining closed-form inference. We further introduce HEB average one-dependence estimators (HEB-AODE), showing that the adaptive smoothing transfers cleanly to structural relaxations of NB. Theoretically, we establish a non-asymptotic $\ell_1$ error bound for HEB-NB matching the empirical-distribution minimax rate plus a vanishing data-adaptive bias, together with a matching Laplace-tight lower bound that yields a finite-sample, risk-level strict separation from Laplace. We further derive a plug-in excess Bayes-risk bound via total-variation tensorization and a population top-1 expected calibration error (ECE) corollary. Empirically, across 31 UCI and OpenML benchmarks, HEB-NB attains the best average Friedman rank on probabilistic metrics, with up to 22.1% log-loss reductions on high-cardinality datasets and consistent improvements of HEB-AODE over vanilla AODE. Combining HEB-NB with mutual-information weighting reduces top-1 ECE by 41%-70%, demonstrating substantial gains in probabilistic accuracy and calibration.

AI.tldr: HEB-NB introduces hierarchical empirical Bayes smoothing for Naive Bayes classifiers with adaptive concentration parameters, outperforming fixed smoothing methods on high-cardinality tabular data with better probabilistic accuracy and calibration.
AI.motivation: Standard smoothing methods for Naive Bayes classifiers (Laplace, Lidstone, etc.) use fixed smoothing strengths that ignore important data characteristics like feature cardinality, sample size, and class imbalance. This causes non-vanishing bias on modern high-cardinality tabular data.
AI.method: Proposes hierarchical empirical-Bayes Naive Bayes (HEB-NB) where each class-feature conditional probability is smoothed by a Dirichlet prior whose concentration is learned adaptively via Type-II maximum likelihood. Also extends to HEB average one-dependence estimators (HEB-AODE).
AI.result: HEB-NB achieves best average Friedman rank on 31 UCI/OpenML benchmarks with up to 22.1% log-loss reduction on high-cardinality datasets. Combined with mutual-information weighting, reduces top-1 expected calibration error by 41-70%.
AI.conclusion: HEB-NB provides principled adaptive smoothing that significantly improves probabilistic accuracy and calibration over traditional fixed smoothing methods, with theoretical guarantees and practical empirical performance.

title: Beyond a Bag of Features: Set-Level Instability in Sparse Autoencoders
summary: Shani et al. (2026) show that LLM representations broadly recover human category boundaries, while failing to reflect fine-grained typicality structure. Their analysis uses cosine similarity over dense model representations. We revisit their approach using overlap over active sparse autoencoder (SAE) latent sets as a more interpretable similarity measure. We first verify that this set-level measure is meaningful: SAE latent sets can recover union-like compositional structure in controlled toy models and induce semantically coherent neighborhoods in natural text. Extending the human-concepts analysis to SAE set similarities, we find that SAE activation sets do not recover human category boundaries or within-category typicality more faithfully than dense embeddings or residual-stream states, but instead track model-internal similarity structure. To probe this gap further, we study active latent sets under well-controlled semantic modifications, revealing a substantial mismatch between human judgements of conceptual change and change in the SAE active set. We interpret this as evidence that, outside idealised settings, SAE features do not compose via simple bag-of-features semantics.

AI.tldr: SAE set similarity doesn't recover human category boundaries better than dense embeddings; reveals gap between human conceptual judgments and model-internal similarity structure
AI.motivation: Previous work (Shani et al., 2026) showed LLM representations recover human category boundaries but fail at fine-grained typicality. The authors want to revisit this analysis using SAE latent sets as a more interpretable similarity measure to see if this reveals better alignment with human concepts.
AI.method: Used overlap over active sparse autoencoder (SAE) latent sets as similarity measure. Verified method with controlled toy models showing SAE latent sets recover union-like compositional structure. Extended human-concepts analysis to SAE set similarities on natural text data.
AI.result: SAE activation sets do not recover human category boundaries or typicality better than dense embeddings/residual-stream states. Instead track model-internal similarity structure. Found substantial mismatch between human judgements of conceptual change and changes in SAE active set under controlled semantic modifications.
AI.conclusion: SAE features do not compose via simple bag-of-features semantics outside idealized settings. There's a significant gap between human conceptual understanding and model-internal similarity structure as captured by SAE latent sets.

title: Divergent Response Modes in Frontier Language Models Under Steering Pressure
summary: Frontier language models are trained using distinct data, objectives, and safety pipelines. Whether these differences produce measurably different behaviors under explicit steering pressure remains underexplored. This study evaluates behavioral steerability across six frontier models from six developers using 300 paired base and steered items over three categories: values-conflict, reasoning-elicitation, and reasoning-suppression (plus 40 validation items). All six models act as blind peer judges and classify every response based on fixed behavioral rubrics. The resulting 24,480 judgments are scored by leave-one-out consensus. We find that models differ not just in how much steering shifts their behavior but in what kind (mode) of response they give, and some response modes appear in only one or two of them. GPT-5 deflects requests to disclose its reasoning while leaving its answer intact (99% vs. 0% for all other models). Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5 resist explicit suppression instructions and in different ways. Using Llama as the open-weight model, we trace the largest behavioral split to its internals. A linear probe decodes the behavior from the residual stream at 0.87 held-out accuracy while injecting that direction during generation drives the behavior from 0% to 86% across an intervention sweep. Every finding holds under both a token-budget remediation and a control experiment with a hypothesis-blind judgment prompt.

AI.tldr: Frontier language models from different developers show significant differences in behavioral steerability when prompted, with distinct response modes and resistance patterns that vary by model architecture and training.
AI.motivation: Different frontier language models are trained with distinct data, objectives, and safety pipelines, but it remains underexplored whether these differences produce measurably different behaviors under explicit steering pressure.
AI.method: Evaluated behavioral steerability across 6 frontier models using 300 paired base and steered items over 3 categories: values-conflict, reasoning-elicitation, and reasoning-suppression. Used blind peer judging by all models with fixed behavioral rubrics, scoring 24,480 judgments by leave-one-out consensus. Conducted intervention studies with linear probes on Llama's internal representations.
AI.result: Models differ in both degree and mode of response to steering, with unique response patterns appearing in only 1-2 models. GPT-5 deflects reasoning disclosure (99% vs. 0% for others). Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5 resist suppression instructions differently. Linear probe on Llama decodes behavior at 0.87 accuracy; injecting decoded direction drives behavior from 0% to 86% across intervention sweep.
AI.conclusion: Frontier models exhibit fundamentally different behavioral signatures under steering pressure, suggesting that training differences create measurable divergence in how models respond to explicit prompts. These differences hold under various validation methods and can be traced to internal model representations.
